#4621. 3 things you might not know about daylight saving time

Published Oct 31, 2026 1:39 PM EDT

Heads up: The clocks are about to change. The evening of Halloween gets an extra hour as the clocks fall back an hour, meaning you can sleep in on Sunday, November 1.

Complaints about daylight savings are as old as daylight savings itself, and pretty much everyone has an opinion about the practice. As with any such topic, there are all kinds of myths and misunderstandings out there.

This one comes up a lot: the idea that farmers are the reason we have daylight savings. In this version of the story, farmers, who work outside and need to align their workdays with the daylight, were the ones who made the argument for the practice.

In truth, farmers were the main group opposed to daylight savings during World War I. According to the Library of Congress: “The agriculture industry fervently opposed the measure because farming schedules are based on sunrise and sunset not the clock.”

After the war there was a bill to repeal daylight savings, which passed through both houses of Congress. President Woodrow Wilson vetoed that bill, and his statement about the veto acknowledged this wouldn’t make farmers happy.

“I realize the very considerable and in some respects very serious inconveniences to which the daylight-saving law subjects the farmers of the country,” he wrote. Wilson sided with the industrial sector. The veto was overridden, leading to a long period where daylight savings was practiced only in certain areas. For example: New York City observed daylight savings, but rural areas in New York State did not (not what you’d expect if farmers broadly supported daylight savings).

None of this is to say that some farmers don’t support daylight savings time today—it’s just that farmers aren’t the reason the practice exists in America. If anything, they tried to stop it.

There are some “facts” repeated so often that hardly anyone questions them, and “Ben Franklin invented daylight savings time” remains one of them. The problem is that it’s not true.

I’d understand if you’re skeptical—I’m a Canadian journalist trying to steal an achievement from one of America’s founding fathers. But you don’t have to take my word on this one—The Franklin Institute, a museum dedicated to Franklin’s legacy, states that “Daylight saving time is one thing that Franklin did not invent.” The United States didn’t even implement daylight savings until 1918, well over a century after Franklin passed away.

So where did the idea that he invented it come from? Probably from a satirical Journal de Paris article Franklin penned back in 1784.

In that piece he jokingly encouraged the residents of Paris to wake up earlier in the morning, in order to spend less money on candles. He also proposed a tax on shutters, rationing of candles, a prohibition of carriages on the streets after sunset, and church bells ringing at the crack of dawn every day. He, it goes without saying, wasn’t being entirely serious.

So where did the idea for daylight savings come from? New Zealand entomologist George Hudson first proposed intentionally shifting the clock in an 1895 talk to the Wellington Philosophical Society, then followed up with a paper in 1898.

This isn’t a myth, exactly, but it is something that rarely comes up in contemporary discussions about daylight savings. Multiple US states have proposed doing away with standard time entirely. Nationally, the Sunshine Protection Act, which passed the House over the summer, would institute the change from sea to shining sea.

Here’s the thing, though: this isn’t the first time. The US tried making daylight savings permanent during the height of the 1970s energy crisis. The problem was that people hated it. What was supposed to be a two-year experiment lasted less than a year because of a massive change in public opinion.

Support for the change started high, as an October 1974 New York Times article lays out: 79 percent of the public favored the idea in December of 1973, but by February of 1974, that dropped to 42 percent—a 37-point swing. A bill to restore standard time in winter passed the House by a 362 to 16 vote.

What caused the backlash? Dark winter mornings. Particularly prominent were complaints from parents, who didn’t like their children walking to school in the dark.

A 1975 study by the US Department of Transportation concluded that a year-round switch possibly isn’t a great idea, proposing instead a schedule change. “We conclude that modest overall benefits might be realized by a shift from the historic 6-month DST system (May through October) to an 8-month DST system (March through October),” the paper concludes. This, notably, is pretty much what the US has been doing since 2007.

The past isn’t a prediction of the future—it’s possible switching to year-round daylight savings would go differently today. Walking to school is less common, for one thing, and streets are better lit. All the same, it’s worth realizing this has been tried before.

#4620. Jasion Poki review: The Electric Minibike that packs heavy-duty fun

In our transportation reporting, we rarely come across something as fun as today’s review of the Jasion Poki.

The Poki is a severely overpowered electric minibike that looks like it came from yesteryear. If the power isn’t enough, it also packs some cool tricks, and we’re not (just) talking about wheelies this time.

So taking a look at this bad boy, it just screams fun. It is really low to the ground, has a big, wide seat large enough for 2 people as long as they are under 350lbs total, and has pegs for 2 people and a basket, great for carrying a picnic and an extra helmet.

This thing is built like a tank, and it tips the scales accordingly. Getting this thing in my SUV ruptured a few discs in my back, though its compact nature means it fit quite well. Loosen the handlebars and it is downright compact. But that weight is strangely like 50lbs heavier than I would expect at close to 140lbs.

That also makes the built-in wheelies a little bit more suspect. My son, who is by now becoming an expert at wheelies, found this one to be a bit more difficult than the auto wheelies on bikes like the Anyland or new Yozma IN11.

OK so not only does this little powerhouse get you (and your friend) around town in style and it also makes wheelies a bit easier; but it also has a huge Bluetooth speaker in the back that sounds like a Harley and is all synced up with the actual controller so it sounds real.

Sure, it is a gimmick, but it is a fun one, and it might actually make the low-down bike a little safer since it is going to be out of the sight of most cars.

I love this thing. It is my favorite bike to go to the beach on (and it does well in the sand with those fat tires). But I think there are some big misses here. First of all, it has no business going over 40mph. Not only does it feel scary with those tiny wheels, but speed wobbles puts both the rider a possible second rider at significant risk here. This is a fun bike and it should top out at 20-28mph max. Keep all the torque, just cut out the power at a reasonable top speed.

Also it should weigh a lot less. At 140lbs, it is silly hard to get into the back of a car, which it easily fits in. Making the frame aluminum would go a long way here. Also, if this thing rolled on top of you, it would be a bad day.

Make this thing safer and more portable, and I’d recommend everyone with a beach commute to get one. As it stands, best for responsible adults with strong backs and a Peter Pan complex.

The Poki is currently priced at $1,799, and customers can get 5% off with the code Electrek.

#4619. ‘Billie’ Is a 650-HP Modified Pontiac GTO from Ringbrothers

Ringbrothers is back at SEMA with a customized 1965 Pontiac, featuring carbon-fiber bodywork and an LT4 supercharged V-8 engine.

The 2026 SEMA show opened today, celebrating the unbridled imagination of the custom car scene, and, of course, Wisconsin-based Ringbrothers has returned with yet another exquisite creation. This year’s showpiece is a 1965 Pontiac GTO convertible dubbed “Billie,” which enhances the classic muscle car’s assertive styling and packs it with modern power.

Ringbrothers built Billie for a customer who wanted to pay tribute to a GTO his mother once owned. The client originally proposed the name “Goat,” with Ringbrothers suggesting Billie (as in billy goat), a more playful take on the iconic Pontiac’s long-held nickname.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97219

Despite presenting as a GTO, Billie originally started life as a 1965 Pontiac Tempest, before Ringbrothers went to work, widening the body by five inches, reshaping the front fenders, lengthening the rocker panels, and adding carbon-fiber doors. The hood is also fashioned from carbon fiber and wears billet-aluminum inserts and an enlarged scoop to feed air to the engine.

That engine is Chevy’s LT4 supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, cranking out 650 horsepower and 650 pound-feet of torque and hooked up to a Bowler Performance 10-speed automatic transmission. The body is placed atop a Roadster Shop Fast Track Stage III chassis, and Billie also features Fox coil-over springs and six-piston Brembo brakes. The staggered HRE G-Code wheels, measuring 19 inches up front and 20 inches at the rear, are shod in Michelin Pilot Sport Cup 2 rubber.

At first glance, Billie looks quite faithful to the original GTO, but look closely, and you’ll notice custom bumpers, new headlight surrounds, and a single-piece machined billet-aluminum taillight panel. Ringbrothers also employed carbon fiber on the lower front end and for the rear bumper section that houses the large exhaust outlets. Adding to the head-turning look is the Billie Goat Blue paint job, a rich, shimmering hue that is contrasted by polished chrome trim.

The cabin is outfitted in gray and blue leather, while the dashboard has been pushed four inches forward and two inches lower. Ringbrothers modernized the instrumentation, fitted a new climate-control system, and added an auto-dimming rearview mirror. There’s also a restored factory radio that now has Bluetooth connectivity, and the aluminum trim is paired with a sweet wood shifter.

Ringbrothers says the entire build took more than 5500 hours. Billie may not be as radical as some of Ringbrothers’ past projects, such as the LT4-powered Rolls-Royce dubbed “Paramount” or “Enyo,” a 1948 Chevy truck turned into an open-wheel race car, but the modified Pontiac is the perfect representation of the company’s expertise in honing the classic lines of vintage muscle cars.

#4617. The Karma Eximius 1 Swaps Its 3-Cylinder Range Extender Engine for 6.2-Liter V-8 Power

That said, it’s a one-off build, so don’t expect to see similar cars at your local Karma dealer.

14 years after the debut of the original Fisker Karma, successor brand Karma Automotive is still trying to build a future beyond that car. It has grand plans to do so with a new two-door GT and an SUV—but in the meantime, the basic Fisker Karma platform is still evolving. The latest Karma model takes the basic shape of the original car to its wildest extreme yet: a one-off called the Eximius 1.

The bright blue sedan retains the basic shape of the Gyesera four-door first unveiled in 2024, but its three-cylinder series hybrid powertrain has been replaced by something substantially more powerful. Karma says that the Eximius 1 features a 6.2-liter V-8 pushing out 550 horsepower, which is paired with 645 hp from its batteries for a peak system output of 1200 ponies. That gets the car from 0-60 miles per hour in a claimed 2.7 seconds, and the brand says that the one-off is complete with carbon ceramic brakes and a semi-active Ohlens suspension to help keep all that power on the road.

While the performance is a huge step up from the Gyesera, the styling changes are even more outrageous. Massive aero elements jut out from the front fenders and rear doors, wrapped in contrasting white to emphasize the widebody look. A front splitter, rear wing, and rear diffuser are all adorned with LED running lights or tail lights, ensuring that the aggressive aerodynamics will be visible at night just as they are in the day.

Inside, the Gyesera’s relatively muted cabin is revamped with a mix of bright blue and white materials. Alcantara appears everywhere from the dashboard to the seats, Recaro buckets in both the front and rear of the car. The rear center console is built around an Eximius-branded carbon fiber helmet, secured in position with a bright blue strap that matches the car’s seatbelts.

Karma is not saying who exactly ordered the Eximius 1, but the brand does add that the number on the side, 5, is “of particular significance to the commissioning client.” Given that it is hard to miss, the owner should be fairly easy to spot the first time they take it out for a drive in public.

#4616. What to do if you hit a deer

Published Oct 31, 2026 2:07 PM EDT

When you think of the fall season, chances are that gorgeous foliage, brisk sweater weather, and Halloween decorations come to mind. Deer, on the other hand, think of sex.

Deer breeding behavior, known as the rut, aligns with the changing length of daylight. As daylight decreases, buck (male deer) and doe (female deer) hormones increase. While in southern states the rut can last several months, it only runs for a short period of time during the fall in the Northeast.

During the rut, bucks seek out does that are ready to breed, and the amorous pursuit can be intense. Because some bucks are so obsessed with breeding, they can eat little and burn through up to 20 percent of their body weight during the season. And just like love-crazed high schoolers, deer during the rut are more distracted and less cautious, as well as more active during the day than they usually are.

“During this period, many yearling bucks leave their birth areas in search of new territory, sometimes dozens of miles away. At the same time, adult bucks are actively roaming their home ranges in pursuit of doe, often chasing those they encounter,” according to Raven Ridge Wildlife Center in Pennsylvania.

What’s more, “The end of daylight-saving time means more vehicles will be on the road during dusk and dawn, which are the peak hours for deer movement.”

In fact, most deer-vehicle accidents take place in October through December. While there are things you can do to lessen your chances of hitting one—such as staying alert and paying close attention when you see deer crossing signs—sometimes accidents are unavoidable. So what should you do if you hit a deer?

Safely pull over and turn your emergency flashers on. While your instinct might be to go see the deer or move the body off of the road, resist the temptation. Care for any injured passengers, and call 911. The dispatchers will send the appropriate authorities to help.

And if you narrowly avoided one deer, remember that, “deer often travel in groups and walk single file,” per the Raven Ridge Wildlife Center. “So even if one deer successfully crosses the road in front of a driver, it doesn’t mean the threat is over. Another could be right behind it.”

#4615. Track-Optimized Fluidity: We Drive the 2027 Ariel Atom 4RR

With 525 horsepower on tap, the no-nonsense Atom 4RR could easily be overwhelming, but it isn’t.

When the Ariel Atom launched around the turn of the millennium, probably no one imagined that the lightweight British track car would evolve into the 4RR model of today—a 525-hp road-legal range topper based on the fourth-generation Atom and launched to celebrate the original’s 25th anniversary. In fact, the roughly 1500-pound “Double R” might be hard for U.S. buyers to conceive of, as only some lesser Ariel vehicles had been available stateside under a manufacturing licensing arrangement.

An exclusive new deal between Ariel and long-standing U.S. distributor Forman Motorworks changes that, with all Ariels and optional equipment now available to order via Forman for U.K. factory build slots. Customer deliveries in the U.S. are planned to start next summer.

The lineup includes the 4RR seen here, which is both the most powerful Atom ever and the most expensive at £208,000 in the U.K. (U.S. prices have yet to be confirmed, but we’d estimate $325,000.) That’s more than double the price of a very generously optioned 400-hp 4R model.

See all results for used cars for sale near 30149

Lower yourself into the Atom’s molded composite driving seat, thumb the start button, and feel the hand-built Civic Type R–derived turbo four-cylinder fizz through the steel-tube-frame chassis. Admittedly, the thought of blasting over the hedged lanes near Ariel’s rural base in Somerset, England, is more than a little intimidating. Yet even as the 4RR accelerates ferociously and telegraphs mechanical and road-surface detail like few other cars can, the big surprise is just how calm this extreme Atom feels.

Whether it’s the car’s refusal to be upset by midcorner bumps and awkward road cambers, or the drivability of the highly boosted turbo four, there’s an unexpected maturity and polish at play here. Even the Quaife six-speed sequential transmission can be soothed with a gentle brush of the clutch pedal. A handful of miles in, and our trepidation has already melted away.

Two things explain the 4RR’s fine road manners. The first is the clearly accomplished setup work overseen by race driver and former Top Gear Stig Phil Keen, and the second is some very expensive engineering.

The latter element includes reworked manually adjustable Öhlins dampers—which allowed Ariel to soften the inboard, pushrod-operated suspension—alongside a new aerodynamics package and 12.2-inch AP Racing brakes with four-piston calipers all around.

But the biggest investment involves the engine. Ariel doesn’t typically touch engine internals, but the 4RR’s previous-generation Civic Type R K20C unit has been completely reworked, blueprinted, and balanced in a process said to consume around 100 hours. Upgrades include forged connecting rods and pistons, closed-deck sleeves, and a revised cylinder head with improved camshafts, valve springs, and guides. A larger turbocharger runs nearly 25 psi of boost and is fed by an intercooler about twice the size of the 4R’s.

See all results for used cars for sale near 30149

The marquee numbers: 525 horsepower at 8200 rpm and 406 pound-feet of torque at 5200 revs. However, two tamer performance maps let you ease into it; there’s a 4R-matching 400-hp tune, as well as an intermediate 500-hp setting. Traction control and ABS are included and very welcome, both being driver adjustable through multiple stages, including fully off.

For such a small turbo four capable of producing so much power, the 4RR is disarmingly flexible at low revs and surprisingly progressive when it comes on boost, partly thanks to peak torque arriving at a far higher engine speed than in most modern turbocharged road cars.

That’s true in both the first two engine maps (despite the very noticeable step up in performance, including the intermediate map’s more substantial midrange boost), but it’s the seemingly modest 25-hp increase to the third and most powerful tune that transforms the experience. Still progressive and really quite tractable, it’s the searing, angry spit toward the 8200-rpm rev limiter that’s most noticeable, along with equally furious overrun pops. Throw in a few full-throttle, clutchless upshifts, and this amounts to delirious performance that—while usable on the road—is best reserved for an open racetrack.

Even then, traction from the 255-section rear tires is astonishing, at least in the hot, dry conditions of our drive. Whether launched off the line or subjected to a surge of midrange torque, the 4RR simply digs in and grips, thanks in no small part to compliant damping, sticky Yokohama A052 track-oriented rubber, and the weight of that Honda four pressing the rear tires into the tarmac.

Back-to-back drives in the 4RR and one of the first Atoms underlines the comedic jump in performance, but it’s the finesse of the 4RR chassis that’s more revealing of the car’s quarter century of development. Delightfully tactile as the original is, each individual wheel jiggles over bumps, and the car quickly becomes unstable if you back out of the throttle midcorner.

The 4RR retains comparable tactility but dials out the chassis noise and lifts the Atom’s capabilities to another level. The steering is super responsive but refuses to tug over tricky surfaces, the car’s balance is throttle adjustable but more forgiving of midcorner lifts, and crushing braking performance tames the engine’s power without causing the front axle to weave. For a circuit-optimized machine, the 4RR is exceptionally fluid on the road.

It’s easy to get caught up in the 4RR’s extreme nature and its hypercar-like power-to-weight ratio, but the real takeaway is how thoroughly Ariel has harnessed its intensity, creating a car that feels engineered around its performance, not overwhelmed by it.

#4614. Waymo picks Toyota bZ4X as its next robotaxi, starting in Japan in 2027

Waymo is adding the Toyota bZ4X to its robotaxi lineup. Toyota will build a custom version of the electric SUV with the Waymo Driver integrated right on the line in Japan, and a test fleet will start operating there in 2027.

It’s the first actual vehicle to come out of the partnership the two companies signed last year. And it gives Waymo a Japanese-built car for its Tokyo launch, with the UK and other markets to follow.

When Waymo and Toyota first announced their deal in April 2025, it was a preliminary agreement to “explore” working together on autonomous driving, including in personally owned vehicles. Lots of intent, no product.

Now there’s a product. According to Waymo’s announcement, Toyota will produce the vehicles at its Takaoka plant in Toyota City, Aichi Prefecture, and Waymo’s self-driving hardware will be installed and integrated at that same site instead of being retrofitted somewhere else.

The robotaxi bZ4X gets a few rider-focused changes: extra rear legroom, automatic doors, a power liftgate, and ambient lighting. Waymo didn’t share sensor specs, unit volumes, or what each vehicle costs.

Operations in 2027 are about testing and validating the autonomous bZ4X fleet in Japan. The UK and “other Waymo markets” come in later years, with no dates attached.

The two companies also say they’ll keep working on autonomous tech for Toyota’s personal vehicles, plus safety projects with Woven by Toyota, the automaker’s software arm.

Waymo co-CEO Dmitri Dolgov said that “Toyota’s commitment to zero traffic accidents resonates deeply with us at Waymo.”

The timing lines up with Waymo’s Japan plans. In September, Waymo said it’s targeting fully driverless commercial rides in Tokyo in 2027 with taxi operator Nihon Kotsu and ride-hailing app GO, scaling to about 100 vehicles, pending regulatory approval.

In the US, Waymo’s fleet is still mostly made up of Jaguar I-Pace SUVs, a model Jaguar no longer produces. It’s been adding the Zeekr-built Ojai van and the Hyundai Ioniq 5, and Hyundai is reportedly in talks to supply up to 50,000 Ioniq 5 robotaxis by 2028.

The bZ4X makes four. It isn’t Toyota’s first robotaxi bZ4X either: Toyota and Pony.ai started mass-producing bZ4X-based robotaxis in China earlier this year.

For US readers, the refreshed model is sold here simply as the Toyota bZ, starting at $34,900. A cheap, high-volume base vehicle matters a lot when you’re trying to scale a fleet.

And Waymo is scaling. It now does over 500,000 paid rides a week across 15 US metros, and it picked Toronto as its first Canadian city earlier this month, with riders targeted for 2028.

This is a big one, even if the bZ4X is about as exciting as a toaster.

Waymo’s biggest constraint right now is cars. It has been running a fleet built on a discontinued Jaguar, and every new automaker it signs adds manufacturing capacity it doesn’t have to build itself. Toyota is the world’s best-selling automaker. Having it build Waymo-ready vehicles on its own assembly line is exactly the kind of industrial partner Waymo needed.

If Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning a personal vehicle, they are likely working on it. It doesn’t mean that it is going to happen but it’s obviously an avenue that they are both willing to explore. If things work out and they are actually able to bring a fully autonomous vehicle to market, that’s an extremely significant advantage from a top legacy car manufacturer that ultimately changes the game for Toyota and could potentially put them in the middle of the competition with other EV manufacturers.

Yes, the bZ4X had a rough start (Toyota recalled the first batch in 2022 because the wheels could come off). But it has come a long way now – becoming boring and reliable. And for a robotaxi, boring and reliable is the whole point.

Compare that with Tesla’s approach: a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel, built in-house, with a self-certified autonomy stack that still isn’t operating at anything close to Waymo’s scale. Waymo keeps plugging its driver into existing EVs from established automakers and expanding city by city. So far, that’s working.

The way it is looking now. It sounds like Toyota will take over manufacturing Waymo driver cars for right-hand-drive markets. But what interests me most is the personal-vehicle angle. Toyota and Waymo keep mentioning it, but there’s still nothing concrete. If Toyota actually puts the Waymo Driver in a car you can buy, Tesla’s FSD Supervised pitch gets a lot harder to sell. Will that happen before the end of the decade? Who knows.

#4613. Putrid blood shoots from these lizards’ eyes

Published Nov 1, 2026 8:03 AM EST

Horned lizards are spiky cuties. Three to six inches long, these lizards are coated with sharp spines all across their hard, sand-colored backs. But in the dry deserts and prairies they call home, they are still vulnerable. As they scuttle through the protective brush in arid landscapes from Mexico to southern Canada, they have to reckon with hungry coyotes, snakes that will gobble them whole, and even peckish roadrunners. That’s why multiple species of horned lizards have developed a weird but effective deterrent: blood.

And not just any blood: These lizards shoot foul-smelling blood out of their eyes, sending many would-be predators scattering. But experts say the lizards are now facing other threats to their survival that even a fountain of eye blood can’t deter.

Dean Williams, a professor of biology at Texas Christian University, studies horned lizard populations in central Texas. He says that blood squirting is really a backup defense for the lizards. “Their first line of defense is going to be crypsis,” aka blending in with their background, says Williams.

Williams and his colleagues tag the lizards they study with radio trackers that pinpoint their location to an area roughly the size of an office desk. Even then, he says, it can take “15 minutes of rummaging” to find the lizard in their scrubland habitat. The lizards don’t move much, he added, blending in with nearby rocks.

But when hiding doesn’t work, the lizards deploy their unusual, foul-smelling blood, which Williams says is a product of an equally foul delicacy. “Their diet consists mainly of these large Pogonomyrmex or harvester ants,” says Williams. Harvester ants defend themselves using neurotoxic venom that causes intense, long-lasting, stinging pain in mammals.

Unfortunately for the harvester ants, this toxin doesn’t even slightly deter horned lizards, who eat the ants in large numbers. A 2024 study identified that a compound in the lizards’ blood spiked after scientists fed them harvester ants. The researchers think this compound, possibly adapted from ant venom, makes the lizards’ blood taste foul.

However, that gross metabolized ant blood coursing through the lizards’ veins wouldn’t be much help if it only annoyed a predator after it had already bitten off the lizard’s head. That’s where the lizards’ unusual squirting mechanism comes in handy.

Williams explains that the lizards can build up pressure in blood vessels around their sinuses. Eventually, the vessels burst, shooting the toxic blood out in jets. Mammals exposed to the stream of blood react with notable disgust. There seems to be little consequence for the lizards, even though in one experiment, a lizard lost 6.8 percent of its body mass after squirting blood when exposed to a dog.

The foul-smelling blood doesn’t protect the lizards from every predator, though. Roadrunners and other birds of prey still chow down on them, says Williams. To guard against birds, the lizards use the sharp horns on the back of their heads to stab at predators that try to seize them in their beaks.

The lizards’ foul blood also does little to deter snakes. Instead, the lizards have evolved specialized strategies to evade these predators. Rattlesnakes are lazy hunters that wait in the shadows for prey to approach. Horned lizards have learned to run away from these snakes.

But Williams says they use a different strategy if hunted by a coachwhip or racer snake. These fearsome snakes can easily chase down the lizards, who instead quickly flatten their bodies against the dirt, showing the snake their spiked backs, which makes them harder to swallow.

But despite these bespoke, often ingenious defense mechanisms, horned lizards in the Lone Star State are under serious threat. They’ve disappeared from their habitat across eastern Texas. Williams says that industrialization is devastating lizard populations. “They seem to be very sensitive to those habitat changes,” he says.

In small towns, the lizards can live alongside humans when their natural brush habitat is preserved. But in towns where humans cleared the brush, “the lizards just disappeared,” Williams says.

Horned lizards are ectotherms, meaning they must change their behavior to keep their body temperature under control. In the blistering heat of a Texas summer, the lizards simply can’t keep their bodies within safe limits once the cool shade of vegetation has disappeared.

Harvester ants provide horned lizards with one of their strongest defenses. But another ant species has become the second major challenge to the lizards’ survival. Fire ants are an invasive species in the United States. They swarm the nests of ground-dwelling lizards, eating vulnerable eggs, or even attacking and killing young lizards.

That’s where conservation efforts, like the one Williams works on with zoos across Texas, play an important role. The program releases nearly a thousand young lizards each year.

These hatchlings, which can easily fit in the palm of a hand, are packaged in individual Tupperware containers and then released in the desert scrub. Williams says that his graduate student, Kira Gangbin, has been working on a targeted poison to cut down fire ant numbers and help keep these hatchlings alive. These efforts will hopefully keep horned lizard populations thriving for many more years. Just remember: If you come across a horned lizard on a hike through the Texas desert, give it a wide berth, or risk a foul, bloody surprise.

#4612. Acura Kicks Off Sales Of More Than 3000 Official Reproduction Parts for the 1st-Gen NSX

Acura’s NSX heritage parts program moves from announcement to U.S. sales, giving owners fresh support for their aging supercars.

Buying or owning an older supercar is one thing. Keeping it on the road is another issue, and that's only complicated further when it comes to finding replacement parts. Acura is now making that aspect of ownership about as easy as it could possibly be for first-gen NSX owners: as of Monday, the brand is officially kicking off sales of more than 3000 reproduction parts through its Honda Heritage Parts program.

The new welcome development for NSX owners comes through Acura dealerships nationwide and through Honda's DreamShop. The reality here is that, although great cars like the NSX have exceptional enthusiast support, factory-backed parts recreation is hard to match. It's one thing to hope you'll find a part across used listings and another to know it's available at a local dealer.

If all this sounds familiar, it's for good reason. As Road & Track reported in March, the company has been intending to bring reproduction parts to American dealers for a minute now. This latest development moves the story along to actual sales. That said, there are two very clear sides to this business: “Genuine Honda Reproduction Parts” use the same materials and production methods as the original components; “Honda Compatible Parts” are redeveloped replacements for original pieces that the company no longer sells.

That differentiation allows the brand to build what it feels makes sense and lean on suppliers elsewhere. Originally, Acura said it would cover the powertrain, interior, exterior, electrical, and chassis components. That's a wide swath to be sure—but for now, owners will still need to check availability to be sure that the individual piece they need is available.

That said, all of this signals just how key the NSX is to Acura and Honda. Supporting a supercar decades after production helps owners keep and maintain the car in question. In addition, it gives prospective buyers a touch more confidence about picking one up. In other words, it could boost the second-hand market and the overarching value of the nameplate itself. That won't make an NSX (or any other supercar) cheap or easy to maintain, but it eases some of the frustration.

#4611. Volkswagen hits pause on the Golf EV as it faces an ‘urgent need for action’

Volkswagen has put the electric Golf on hold for now as it faces growing pressure to cut costs.

“We cannot afford to lose any time and must act quickly and decisively,” Volkswagen Group CFO and COO Arno Antlitz warned after the company reported its largest quarterly loss since the “Dieselgate” scandal in 2015 on Thursday.

VW Group’s operating loss swelled to €5.9 billion ($6.5 billion) in the third quarter because of a write-down of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and lower profit margins on electric vehicles.

As part of its latest cost-control efforts, Volkswagen is pausing development of the all-electric Golf at its Wolfsburg plant in Germany.

“We simply can’t afford this work right now,” VW brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said in an internal memo Reuters reviewed on Friday. The Wolfsburg plant, or the “heart of the VW brand,” is about €300 million ($334.5 million) short of its cost-cutting targets, the memo said.

Schäfer said the “decision was really not an easy one for us,” knowing what the Golf means to Wolfsburg.

The decision comes after Volkswagen’s Supervisory Board approved its restructuring strategy, “Future Plan 2030,” last month, which includes reducing its global workforce by 100,000, trimming its lineup, and closing several plants in Germany.

Volkswagen initially planned to launch the Golf EV in 2028, but Schäfer confirmed earlier this year that the electric hatch will be delayed until closer to 2030.

It should be noted that they paid out dividends of 2.6 billion in August. Most of it went to 3 majority shareholders. But they used a clever accounting trick to delay the losses till now, just before talks with unions about pay.

Schäfer suggested the delay was because the SSP (Scalable Systems Platform), developed through its partnership with Rivian, was taking longer than expected.

The electric Golf, which is expected to arrive as the ID. Golf, will be one of the first vehicles based on the new platform.

While development is on hold, VW’s works council said the pause will not delay the Golf EV’s launch, promising to make up for lost time. It’s still expected to launch in 2030.

Volkswagen will begin building the electric Golf in Wolfsburg closer to the end of the decade, while production of the gas-powered model will move to Mexico in 2027.

#4609. Fierce turtles square off in a rare woodland turf battle

Published Nov 1, 2026 10:10 AM EST

At first, it appears that two turtles with yellow spots are calmly sitting side by side. Suddenly, one of them turns, slowly—and lunges out with its head, its open beak clearly trying to take an aggressive chomp out of its neighbor. Moments later, the turtle tries again. Now, both reptiles are going head-to-head, though each is retracted into the protection of its shell.

The two combatants are male eastern box turtles (Terrapene carolina carolina) competing for dominance. Eastern box turtles are a subspecies of the common box turtle (Terrapene carolina), with bright orange and yellow coloring on its dark shell. They live throughout the eastern and midwestern United States.

“I wouldn’t say that they’re normally aggressive, but male box turtles can definitely become territorial, especially since males’ home ranges (the area they frequently occupy) often overlap,” Eamon Caffrey, the turtle research coordinator at Mass Audubon who captured the video, tells Popular Science. “We do occasionally see this sort of brawling behavior between two males when out in the field; you just have to get lucky enough to actually witness it. This experience was a first for me, and I was thrilled to capture it on camera.”

Over the summer, another Mass Audubon staff member saw two male box turtles opting for a pushing contest instead of biting. At one point, one of the two flipped the other contestant onto its back and pushed him down a small hill. Box turtle battles can also feature spinning each other around.

“From my understanding, fights between male box turtles are much more opportunistic than anything else,” Caffrey tells Popular Science. “Often, when two males come in contact, they will display a variety of aggressive behaviors that can include head butting, shell ramming, biting, pushing, and shoving – all in attempts to assert dominance. These disputes are often territorial but can be over mates as well.”

What’s more, the turtle with the darker shell is a well-known individual over 30 years old. Caffrey says he’s seen him various times this year, and since capturing the video the celebrity reptile has been spending time in an area where the Mass Audubon team frequently spot two to three adult females. However, there’s been no trace of his opponent.

“Does that mean he ‘won’ the battle?” Caffrey muses. “Who knows.”

#4608. Hyundai launches the new IONIQ 6 in the UK with up to 422 miles of range, starting at $45K

The new Hyundai IONIQ 6 is now on sale in the UK with an impressive range of up to 422 miles, starting at about $45,000.

Hyundai opened orders for the all-new IONIQ 6 in the UK, starting at £33,240 ($45,000), including the Electric Car Grant (ECG).

The “evolved” electrified streamliner brings a sharp new design, a refined interior, and a bigger battery for longer range.

Hyundai “enhanced every line and detail” for a cleaner, stronger silhouette. The front includes a redesigned shark nose and slim daytime running lights, while the black lower body garnish now extends into the doors.

The rear features a new extended ducktail design replacing the previous generation’s prominent spoiler.

Inside, Hyundai overhauled the new IONIQ 6’s interior with a redesigned two-tone leather steering wheel, a digital side mirror, and a “bridge-type” center console that includes a wireless phone charger and physical buttons.

It includes Hyundai’s new infotainment setup, including dual 12.3″ navigation and infotainment screens with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto capabilities.

In the UK, the new IONIQ 6 is available in three trims: Premium, N-Line, and N-Line Evo, with 225 horsepower RWD or 320 horsepower AWD powertrains.

The base Hyundai IONIQ 6 Premium uses a new 84 kWh battery with the 225 hp RWD powertrain, delivering up to 422 miles of range and 4.6 miles/kWh efficiency.

It starts at £33,240 with the ECG. It includes 18″ alloy wheels, flush auto door handles, dual-zone climate control, heated front seats, heated steering wheel, heat pump, smart regenerative braking, wireless phone charging, over-the-air updates, and the full suite of key safety systems.

The IONIQ 6 N-Line starts at £36,240, including the ECG, and adds a more dynamic N-Line exterior and interior design.

Upgrading to the range-topping N-Line Evo costs £43,270 and adds features like leather and suede seat trim, a suede headliner, front relaxation seats, ventilated front seats, an electric sunroof, and a head-up display.

Other added features included with the N-Line Evo trim include Surround View Monitor, Remote Smart Parking Assist, Parking Collision Avoidance Assist, Digital Key 2, Walk-Away Lock, exterior Vehicle-to-Load adaptor, and BOSE premium audio.

Both the IONIQ 6 N-Line and N-Line Evo use the 84 kWh battery, providing up to 364 miles of driving range in RWD and up to 354 miles with the AWD powertrain.

Beautiful car, very efficient and from what I read, very comfortable. I had my eyes set on it, but the small trunk was a dealbreaker for me. So I went for the EV6, which is maybe even more of a stunner (in the eyes of the beholder) but admittedly significantly less efficient.

Thanks to its 800-volt electrical architecture, the IONIQ 6’s battery can charge from 10% to 80% in about 18 minutes at DC fast-charging speeds of up to 350 kW.

The new IONIQ 6 is now available to order on Hyundai UK’s website, with deliveries set to begin in early 2027.

Sadly, those in the US will miss out on the new-and-improved electrified streamliner. Hyundai is discontinuing the standard IONIQ 6 in the US after the 2026 model year, while the performance N will remain on sale.

#4607. One Wild Genius Built a Supercharged 6-Speed-Stick Nissan Pathfinder for the Track

Nismo Nick's ‘Trackfinder’ pairs a supercharged V-6 with a six-speed manual. Its V-8-powered ‘Trailfinder’ sibling prefers to head off-road.

A body-on-frame, three-row Pathfinder shouldn't be on anyone's track car list. Even with the addition of a supercharger, a six-speed manual gearbox, and a claimed 501 horsepower, it's still not worthy of track time. That said, it is worthy of attention. Arizona Nissan enthusiast and influencer Nick Sherr has built just such an SUV for the 2026 SEMA Show. And on top of that, he's built a much more "appropriate for the situation" V-8-powered off-road companion.

Known online as Nismo Nick, Sherr built what he's calling the Trackfinder and Trailfinder to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the Pathfinder. Both use the R51-generation Pathfinder platform, but each gets comprehensive body and interior changes, with the most obvious being the visual links to the current D41-gen Nissan Frontier. That said, the changes underneath are the most important.

The Trackfinder will make you want to find a helmet. Under the hood is a VQ40 V-6 with a Z1 Off-Road supercharger and an UpRev tune. The team claims 501 horsepower at the wheels—so, sure, we don't have a crankshaft power figure, but it's making somewhat close to double what the stock car makes at said crank.

Getting power from the engine to the tires is a six-speed manual gearbox with a Centerforce clutch and flywheel. Sherr says the GMC Typhoon served as inspiration here, and that makes plenty of sense. The supporting hardware includes roll-forged wheels, Goodyear Eagle F1 All-Season tires, and a Seibon carbon-fiber hood. Nismo-inspired graphics and quad exhaust outlets complete the package.

“I wanted something that would make people laugh, smile, and question everything they thought they knew about a Pathfinder,” Scherr said in the release. Notably—and perhaps unsurprisingly—the debut comes without any notable performance figures or lap times. This is, after all, a concept meant for little more than show.

The Trailfinder does a better job of leaning into what the Pathfinder was intended to do. It picks up a VK56 V-8, and then adds a Z1 Off-Road Titan-swap X-Pro suspension, a big brake kit, an aftermarket intake, and a snorkel. 35-inch Hankook Dynapro AT2 Xtreme tires, rock sliders, and Hammerhead Armor bumpers round out the major components, while Rigid Industries lighting adds another off-road-centric touch.

Sherr has built several Nissan projects that feel like they come from a universe where the brand catered to fans better. The question is, will either or both of these will influence the automaker itself?

#4606. Toyota reveals five new lifted Woodland concepts, including the bZ electric SUV

Toyota introduced a new family of lifted, “adventure-ready” Woodland concepts based on the RAV4, Grand Highlander, Sienna, Crown Signia, and bZ electric SUV.

Toyota is the latest automaker to chase the highly profitable off-road market in the US, with plans to expand its “Woodland” lineup.

Although it already sells Woodland versions of the RAV4, Sienna, bZ, and most recently, the Grand Highlander, Toyota said the new family of concept vehicles is “designed for drivers who see adventure not as a destination, but a way of life.”

Toyota’s North American design studio, CALTY Design Research, designed the concepts to explore how some of its most popular nameplates can be used better on and off the road.

Each vehicle features Horizon Blue exterior paint, inspired by Toyota’s 1960s models, including the Stout, Crown, and Corona.

All new concepts also include an exclusive Woodland badge, plus a lift kit, large over-fenders, satin-black wheels, All-Terrain tires, two-tone paint on the roof and hood, a roof rack, and cross bars to top it off.

According to Toyota, the RAV4 Woodland Plug-In Hybrid and Sienna Woodland Concepts show how its “electrified and family-focused vehicles take on a more adventurous role.”

The electric Woodland bZ Concept “extends the Woodland theme into Toyota’s battery electric future.” Meanwhile, the Grand Highlander Woodland Concept and Crown Signia Woodland Concept bring two distinct models to the lineup, Toyota said.

The company didn’t reveal any powertrain specs or other details, but said the concepts show how capability can take many forms, including PHEV, hybrid, and battery electric.

Toyota’s new Woodland Concepts will be on display at the 2026 SEMA Show, starting on November 3.

To give you an idea, the 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland comes standard with a dual-motor all-wheel-drive (AWD) powertrain, delivering a combined 375 horsepower. That’s an extra 37 hp compared to the standard bZ with AWD.

And for a mere 10-15% reduction in efficiency, our beautiful American suburbanites can Look Butch as they drive about town. Hopefully Toyota offers a package that attaches a shovel and some jerry cans to complete the image.

The bZ Woodland also adds off-road capabilities with 8.3″ of ground clearance and the ability to tow up to 3,500 lbs.

Other rugged upgrades include All-Terrain tires, black side molding, roof rails, and black wheel arch cladding.

The 2027 Toyota bZ Woodland is available in Base and Premium trims, starting at $45,380, or over $10,000 more than the standard bZ.

#4605. How to build an air purifier in 6 simple steps

Published Nov 1, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Though invisible itself, the air we breathe is a microcosm of identifiable pollen, fungal spores, viruses, dust particles, and fine particles of human pollution from everything from cars to asphalt sidewalks. It’s not something we should obsess over day to day, but as more people measure air quality on their own, many are getting readings they’d prefer to address. However, not everyone wants to buy an air purifier, which can cost several hundred dollars.

One proposed solution for at-home air filtration is to use readily available materials like cardboard, box fans, square HVAC filters, and everyone’s favorite building material: duct tape. I did a version of this myself for PopSci, and, though I have mixed feelings about the process, I’m overall satisfied with the result. Here, we’ll go through what I built, how I built it, and my overall conclusions after using it, along with resources for anyone interested in reading further.

There are several configurations for making your own air purifier at home. One of the most documented is a Corsi-Rosenthal box, or CR box for short. It’s essentially an air filter cube, which is what I’ll be calling mine, with four sides made of furnace filters and one side made of a standard box fan (seen above). The fan pulls air through the filters and pushes out cleaner air than came in.

The United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) provides a lot of information about DIY air cleaners, including visual construction guides, tips on improving DIY air cleaners, and general air cleaner usage advice. EPA research on DIY air cleaners for wildfire smoke will also inevitably interest those in wildfire-prone areas who don’t want to purchase an air purifier for smoke.

These resources were used extensively throughout this project. Instead of using this guide as a total replacement for these resources, use this page as a waypoint for how an individual or student group might use one of these devices, with practical concerns highlighted along the way.

I went to my local Walmart and bought a Lasko box fan, two pairs of Filtrete 20-inch MERV 11 furnace filters, and a roll of Duck Brand General Purpose Masking Tape. This represents what a typical consumer might buy without specialty ordering options or bulk purchasing. The total came to $73.58 before taxes and $78.36 after Florida state sales tax.

The box fan, or any fan in a roughly square housing, should be a modern ETL- or UL-listed fan (clearly marked on the box) because older fans and those not ETL- or UL-listed may have issues when run facing upward. This is a safety issue and should not be skipped.

Since the cardboard box your fan comes in will likely become part of your air filter cube, it’s worth getting one that isn’t damaged, though you can tape over small tears.

EPA guidance recommends MERV13 or equivalent filters for the best experience. The MERV scale indicates how much and what kinds of particles the device can filter. High-tier MERV filters can be costly, so I opted for MERV11 since I was able to get a fairly good deal (around $23) per two-pack of these panels, and the notable difference between MERV11 and MERV13 was that the latter can handle forest fire smoke particles, which is not an issue in my area.

You can assemble your air filter cube in less than an hour, even with one person. Rather than a strict job that requires exhaustive measuring and cutting, it’s more of an approximate job that relies on the magic of tape to do the heavy lifting. This is a feasible parent-and-child project for those 6+ and a solo project for those 10+.

For this project, we want air to flow in through the filters and out through the fan. That means that the part of the fan that blows air out needs to be on the exterior of your cube, and the back side of the fan that pulls in air needs to be on the inside of your cube. Like a surgeon marking which limb to operate on before making the first cut, I marked the interior of my fan with ‘I’s for safety. Meanwhile, your filters should have arrows. Those arrows should point towards the inside of the cube.

Place two filters together and use a small piece of tape to connect them as shown. Remember to have the arrows pointing inwards. Continue taping the filters until you form a square. You can either use two people here or secure one filter vertically with a trash bin to do it solo.

The resulting square will be flimsy and contain cracks that air can get through. Tape the seams with duct tape. Don’t worry about being imperfect on the first try. In fact, going over the seams multiple times will only make your cube more secure and airtight.

At this point, your square of filters should be feeling more and more structurally sound. You can now flip it over and repeat the simple taping method from Step 2 on the side that was previously on the ground.

Remember, the box is an important part of the final product. If you place your square over the box, you’ll see they’re roughly the same size. Carefully cut out the most structurally sound side of the box and trim it to be roughly the size of your filter square. It won’t need to be perfect. I used scissors for this, as if imitating a school project, but a standard box cutter or multitool with a cutting edge would be better.

When done, tape the cardboard to one end of your filter square. Your air filter cube now has a bottom.

As a last step, take the fan and put it on the top side of the box, taping it down carefully. If your fan has rounded corners, tape those too. If you notice small gaps in the fan housing, you can seal them with tape, provided they aren’t ventilation openings or near electrical components.

At this point, you have a completed air filter cube. With the fan side up, plug it into an outlet and turn the fan on. Look for structural integrity, a smooth spinning blade with no obstructions from tape or cardboard, and no unusual sounds or vibrations. I recommend being around your new filter cube for a bit before leaving it unattended. Follow any fan manufacturer guidance about long-term or unattended usage.

While I opted not to, you may optionally wish to cover the top of your air filter cube with the cardboard from the other side of the fan box, cutting out a circular hole over the spot where the blades spin. This reduces unintended air recirculation and overall increases the efficiency of the box.

Verdict: Making an air filter cube or CR box is a worthwhile experiment that results in a usable final product, but it may not be the best bang for your buck out there.

After having run my air filter cube for several days now, despite not currently being in possession of an air quality monitor, I can still tell it has worked. For example, there is visible dust on the outside of the filters, which accumulated while I was cleaning dusty gear nearby. Furthermore, neither the grill nor the fan blades themselves are showing the dust that typically accumulates on long-running fans. I would call this project, from an engineering perspective, an obvious success.

Functional mechanics aren’t the only issue, though. Money is time and time is money, and both of these are major issues with these boxes.

One of my biggest complaints about how CR boxes are described to the public is that they are “marketed” as cheap when filters are so expensive. Claims of hyper-cheap CR boxes with EPA-like performance are abundant, though EPA sources use MERV13. My use of MERV11, while reasonable, is another reason to call my creation an air filter cube rather than a true CR box.

Low-cost air purifiers are available commercially that even include HEPA filtration. For example, the Dreo Air Purifier for Home is just $44 right now and, according to Google Chrome’s Shopping Insights tool, despite its $100 MSRP, has never been above $56.

The Dreo air purifier highlights a lot of what feels absent from a DIY air filter cube: a small body you can comfortably place in your home, quiet operation, and filter changes that don’t require completely rebuilding the air purifier every time the filters are used up. For average consumers, I suspect something like the Dreo, or even a larger air purifier like the Levoit Core 300, is going to be a much better option in nearly every way.

Where this really shines is student science. Building your own air filtration cube is fun, sort of like Minecraft block crafting in real life. Students can explore airflow, cost-effectiveness of different materials, and bring home a usable appliance at the end of a one-hour lesson.

I particularly like the idea of students experimenting with different MERV levels, or comparing the effectiveness of low-cost commercial purifiers to their air filtration cubes. Students can, and should, ask themselves at what point the additional health benefits stop justifying the costs in time and money. These sorts of questions are at the core of environmental and healthcare policies that dictate our real world.

#4604. The Car That Fell to Earth: We Test the 1979 Datsun 310-GX

This little Datsun is still getting in touch with reality.

From the May 1979 issue of Car and Driver.

Datsun is not giving up its small-car territory without a fight. All the adver­tising miles on the new 310 are proof of that. For months now, you’ve seen Dat­sun’s new small car zipping across your TV screen, splashed lavishly over maga­zine pages, and blown up bigger than life on roadside billboards. If Datsun is driven to do anything, it’s to sell 310s.

This ad blitz is understandable, be­cause the 310 is Datsun’s new-genera­tion front-wheel-drive car, a key weapon it will use to defend itself in the world­wide small-car war that’s escalating vi­ciously even now. Moreover, it repre­sents Datsun’s second attempt at build­ing a front-drive sedan, since it’s the successor to the ill-fated F-10. As an ac­knowledged small-car giant, Datsun has a reputation to protect.

To these ends, Datsun has armed itself with a pair of all-new three-door se­dans. They’re named simply the 310 se­dan and the 310-GX—which is the sub­ject of this test. A four-door sedan may be sent over later, but for now, just these two constitute the 310 arsenal. The sedan is the family hauler, while the GX is intended to add a dose of sport to the basic 310 theme. For all practical purposes, the two cars are mechanically identical.

See all results for used cars for sale near 30303

The 310 shares its basic layout with the original F-10. It once again has a 1397 cc four-cylinder engine mounted transversely in the chassis and driving the front wheels. Each corner of the unit body is again suspended independently, with MacPherson struts, coil springs, and an anti-sway bar up front, and trail­ing arms and coil springs in the rear. But aside from these superficial similarities to the old F-10, the new 310 is, as they say, new from bumper to bumper.

Which is just fine by us, because the old F-10 just wasn’t suited to life here on spaceship earth. It was, you’ll re­member, an unearthly amalgam of fun­ny shapes and openings, a cramped and noisy little car that always acted a bit tipsy. In fact, given the way the packaging advantages of front-wheel drive were ignored in the F-10, it could well have been designed three thousand miles in outer space instead of that same distance across the Pacific. About the only things you could say in its favor were that its engine, proven in the B-210, was reliable and that it was good in the snow. Not exactly a rave review.

Datsun wants us to forget the past. It's made every attempt to mold the 310 into a car completely different from its predecessor. And if appearances are anything to go by, it’s accomplished that goal. The old banana-with-windows styling has given way to a fresh-cut wedge profile. And while Datsun hasn’t made the 310 any lower, it has made it longer and noticeably wider. For the record, it’s five inches longer and four inches wider, but—at 2600 pounds­—only 80 pounds heavier. Inside, the handsome velour seats, thick carpeting, and color-keyed dash bespeak a new­found awareness of American tastes. And, standard procedure for Japanese carmakers, Datsun has loaded the 310 chock-full of features designed to make life behind the wheel more pleasant.

See all results for used cars for sale near 30303

Every 310, GX or sedan, comes with reclining seats, a split-back folding rear seat, a slider mechanism that moves the passenger’s bucket forward to facilitate rear-seat entry, a quartz clock, a remote hatch opener, side-window defroster vents, intermittent wipers, power brakes, a remote fuel-filler-door open­er, a rear defogger, and a day-night mir­ror. The sedan also features console-­mounted remote cable controls for the flip-out rear windows. The GX adds roll-down rear quarter-windows, a rear window wiper-washer, a tach, a five­-speed transmission, a four-spoke steer­ing wheel, and fatter, 165/70-13 tires. It certainly seems as though Datsun has wedged the 310 right into the heart of small-car country. Yet despite such favorable first impressions, we found—af­ter living with a GX for more than 2000 miles—that all is still not well with Dat­sun’s front-drive car.

The small-car facts of life have been readily defined for Datsun by such front-line front-drivers as the Rabbit, the Strada, the Omni/Horizon, the Fies­ta, the Civic, and now GM’s formidable new X-body compacts. But when you compare it with its competition, the 310 comes off as little more than an F-10 that fell to earth and isn’t quite in touch with reality yet.

The 310’s interior is a perfect exam­ple of the confusing inconsistencies that compromise the car throughout. Datsun obviously went to a lot of trouble to make the 310’s cabin more hospitable than the F-10’s, yet the effect of the handsome carpeting, dash, and uphol­stery is offset by door panels that look plain enough to have come out of a Dat­sun pickup. Datsun also widened the car to achieve more interior width. This al­leviates the phone-booth claustropho­bia of the F-10—but only for front-seat passengers; rear-seat riders are almost as cramped as they were in the older car. In both new cars, rear legroom is still in severely short supply. Other front-drive cars with the same wheel­base do much better in this respect.

Where the GX really falls down on the job is in the all-important area of day-to-day livability. The 310 is so rid­dled with annoying quirks that its posi­tive qualities are overshadowed.

Take the radio, for instance. Please. Our test car had the optional AM/FM unit. Besides impoverished reception, it was endowed with what has to be one of this decade’s worst speakers—mounted under the dash, facing the floor. Most of the music we could tune in became bad­ly garbled when the volume was turned up loud enough to be heard during highway cruising. You don’t have to lis­ten to the radio, of course, but you’ll find the heating system harder to avoid. When you do use it, you’ll find it only marginally effective. Worse yet, the de­froster—which has to work overtime to get the job done—is about as quiet as an idling 747.

And if you want a little whine before dinner, the 310’s trans­mission will be more than happy to oblige—in any gear. Though the 310’s shift linkage is much improved over the F-10’s Silly Putty unit, the transmission crunched almost every time we grabbed third gear. Then there’s the matter of the shift pattern, which has first down and to the left, off of the H, and re­verse—with no protective lockout­—dead ahead, where any self-respecting low gear ought to be. And sure enough, there is the occasional gnashing of re­verse when making the one-two shift.

Then again, we didn’t like reverse much anyway, because selecting it brought on the annoying warning beeper that is Datsun’s fix for the shift-pattern prob­lem. (It’s there to prevent the unwary from backing away from stoplights when they put the shifter where first is in most other cars.) Last but not least was the vibration problem. At idle, the GX’s engine was so rough that the steering wheel actually got a little blurry around the edges. Nudging the idle up about 100 rpm would solve that prob­lem, but only the engineers will be able to quiet the sharp buzzing of the ex­haust system as the revs climb past 5000—a sound that is the essence of tin­niness. Most of these problems also cropped up on a 310 sedan we were sampling, so they seem to be basic de­sign flaws, not isolated failings of the GX test car.

All of this, when added to the below­ average space utilization, makes the 310 rough-edged—even crude—given the current level of small-car sophistication. That’s unfortunate, because it’s due cause for avoiding what is essentially a fun car to drive. The little engine revs up willingly, and the five-speed—top gear is a direct 1:1 ratio—helps you make good use of the available power. The steering response is direct, and there’s plenty of road feel. Once you get used to the suspension’s initial rubberi­ness when you first twist the wheel, the GX turns out to be a fine fling-around car. It’s also quite stable during highway cruising, and it rides acceptably as well. And of course it’s stingy with your gas money, returning 27 miles for every EPA gallon.

But decent road manners are only part of what makes a good small car. The 310 represents a Datsun move in the right direction, but little more; that it’s superior to the F-10 is frankly not one of the world’s outstanding accom­plishments. This is underscored by the fact that $5500 will probably also buy a well-equipped GM X-body compact. And the 310 can’t begin to match the X­ car’s room, ride, quietness, appoint­ments, and overall refinement—yet its economy is only marginally better. The 310 isn’t in the same league.

So at this point the best news we have is that Datsun’s front-drive car has final­ly come down to earth. But if it’s to live here happily, Datsun will have to try still harder—a lot harder.

Since the subject of this test is the 310 sport coupe, I’ll have to add my vote to the negative side. And that’s too bad, be­cause condemning the sport coupe can, by extension, condemn the sedan that came, afterthought-like, with the deal. My strongest negatives about the sport coupe are its looks (really ugly) and its transmission (really terrible). I don’t have either of those complaints about the sedan. In fact, I think Datsun’s marketeers are in for a surprise. Despite their studied predictions, my hunch is the sporty version will be shunned in the showroom (”Yes, Harry. It’s true. It’s the dreaded Show­room Shun”), and the boxy but cute, sim­ple but contemporary sedan will find favor. And that’s the way it should be, be­cause the 310 sedan is—in the Datsun tradition—a functional, sensible, straightfor­ward transportation module, and that’s what a lot of people are looking for these days. They don’t want an overstyled, beeping aggravation. —Mike Knepper

The Datsun 310, like the Subaru, makes us wonder if there is not a streak of automotive perversity loose among America’s car buyers, and if Datsun may not be on to something big. The 310 simply does not address itself to creature comfort in the way that a Toyota or a Honda does. It is a rather Spartan car, with lots of engine and transmission noise, and very little iso­lation from the mechanical realities. There’s an old-fashioned rough-and­-readiness about the 310 that’s not masked by velour upholstery or cut-pile carpets­—a sort of naïve innocence that appealed to me, along with my belief that it would probably run forever—but I couldn’t ex­plain my affectionate regard for these attributes to my co-testers. Noisy little cars that bucket along as the Datsun does are fun. They bring out an adolescent streak in me that 30 years of automotive experi­ence has been insufficient to suppress. They are amusingly likable in their imper­fections—the four-speed sedan more so than the more pretentious coupe. The 310 didn’t try to kid me, nor did it ever let me down. Only when I learned how much I’d have to pay for those simple, earthy pleasures did my enthusiasm start to flag. —David E. Davis Jr.

#4603. The Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept Is a High-Speed Desert-Shredding Machine

But don’t be too surprised to see something like this concept reach showrooms in the next few years.

The Jeep CJ-8 Scrambler of the 1980s took the basic CJ-7, stretched it, and added a pickup bed. Jeep’s latest concept, the Wrangler Scrambler SRT, takes that same formula and ups the ante. Unveiled at the 2026 Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show, the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is not just a body kit on top of a Wrangler frame. Instead, the Wrangler-based concept is the beginning of new developments for the off-road brand, particularly in suspension technology.

The highlight of the concept model is a bespoke high-travel independent front suspension, developed with off-road racing champion Casey Currie. The all-new suspension expands the concept’s performance envelope with enhanced steering precision, wheel control, and high-speed stability. Jeep also added a trophy-truck-inspired rear axle, heavy-duty wheel package, and desert-racing-informed hardware to ensure long-term durability. The suspension architecture first appeared on the Jeep Striker Concept, and was validated by Currie in a custom Jeep Gladiator “Striker” at the NORRA 500.

“The original Scrambler became an icon because it broke the rules. It looked different, worked differently and represented a certain kind of freedom that resonated with enthusiasts then and still does today,” said Tim Kuniskis, head of American brands, SRT Performance, and Direct Connection, Stellantis North America. “We asked ourselves a more provocative question: what happens when SRT stops treating the trail as the limit and builds the ultimate open-air desert weapon? The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is our answer.”

Jeep may have started with a Wrangler chassis, but the final product is not dimensionally similar to a factory JL-generation model. Behind the A-pillar, Jeep added longer doors, custom rear bodywork, an integrated pickup bed, a redesigned tailgate, unique fender flares, and a structural roll cage. Up front, the Wrangler Scrambler features a sharknose design like the Gladiator. (We can’t help but smile at the Punk’n orange paint and bronze-painted beadlock wheels.)

Inside the Wrangler Scrambler, Jeep focused on adaptability. That’s why the rear seats clip securely into floor-mounted hooks and can be removed entirely or rotated to create rear-facing seating. Removing the rear seats allows for storing camping gear, motorcycles, and other adventure equipment without compromise. Dark Graphite leather, orange inserts, contrast stitching, bronze accents, and SRT embroidery adorn the touchpoints of the interior.

Jeep didn’t specify which engine the Scrambler Wrangler uses or detail power figures, but the automaker did leave us some clues about its powertrain. The concept model “honors the original Scrambler” by “imagining how far its rule-breaking formula could be pushed when V-8 power, desert-racing hardware, and SRT performance development are allowed to run without constraint.” That sure sounds like a V-8 engine is under the hood. We’ll cross our fingers that it’s the supercharged 6.2-liter unit out of the Hellcat lineup.

“The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept combines everything enthusiasts love about Jeep vehicles—capability, open-air freedom and authenticity—with the power, control and relentless performance mindset that define SRT,” Kuniskis said. “It is overbuilt and engineered around the idea that the desert can be every bit as demanding as a racetrack. It is unapologetic by design.”

And while this may seem like a flight of SEMA fancy, we suspect it may be a tease for a production car to come. After all, Stellantis’s wide-ranging brand presentation back in May said the carmaker was planning a 2-door Wrangler Scrambler pickup, and that said vehicle would also have an SRT version...
