#4556. Want to become a creative genius? Try this nap hack.

Published Nov 4, 2026 8:30 AM EST

What’s the weirdest thing you learned this week? Well, whatever it is, we promise you’ll have an even weirder answer if you listen to PopSci’s hit podcast. The Weirdest Thing I Learned This Week hits Spotify, YouTube, Apple, and everywhere else you listen to podcasts every-other Wednesday morning. It’s your new favorite source for the strangest science-adjacent facts, figures, and Wikipedia spirals the editors of Popular Science can muster. If you like the stories in this post, we guarantee you’ll love the show.

The internet insists that Edison, Tesla, Einstein, Da Vinci, and Dalí all shared this own cool hack: they napped while holding something heavy, so the clatter would wake them mid-dream and they could grab hold of their unconscious musings before they evaporated. I could only really find a direct source linking such practices to one of them: Dalí. But modern science suggests he may have been on to something.

In 50 Secrets of Magic Craftsmanship, the artist describes “slumber with a key,” which involves a bony Spanish-style armchair, a heavy key, and a plate on the floor. When the key slips out of your fingers and clangs, you wake up. According to Dalí, just a few seconds of slumber could yield priceless creative insights.

There’s some real neuroscience behind this silly-sounding practice, and it comes down to something now known as N1 sleep. As you fall asleep, you pass through N1, the lightest stage of non-REM sleep, where your muscles relax and your brain starts producing dreamlike imagery drawn from your recent experiences. People woken from N1 often swear they were never asleep, yet “microdreams” from these brief siestas can cram elaborate scenes into a few seconds.

Researchers got curious about whether that loose, wandering state could boost creativity. They started with narcolepsy, a condition that involves frequent slips between wake and sleep. They compared 185 patients to 126 typical sleepers and found the narcoleptics scored higher on every creativity measure. The more hybrid-state symptoms they had, the higher the score.

Then, with a strong hunch that this in-between phase could be the key to creativity, they tested N1’s impact directly. Participants worked through a math task with a hidden shortcut, and those who hadn’t found it after 30 rounds took a 20-minute break in a dark room holding a plastic bottle. If they fell asleep and dropped the bottle, they would wake up. Of the 24 who dropped it after reaching N1, 20 (83 percent) found the trick afterward, compared with 15 of 59 (30%) who stayed awake. Even 15 seconds in N1 helped, but dozing deeper erased the benefit.

But unlike Dalí’s reported experiences, people didn’t emerge from N1 with a brilliant idea in tow. The nappers took an average of 94 more trials to crack the math problem. It’s not like they spent their nap time actively working on the math either: the content of their reported N1 dreams had no bearing on how quickly they solved the problem. The link between an N1 wake-up and boosted brainpower was squishier than that, which feels kind of spooky. Listen to this week’s episode to hear more about why we do our best creative work when rudely awoken—and how researchers at MIT are trying to harness this hack.

This week’s episode featured special guest Adam Conover of Adam Ruins Everything fame. He joined the show to talk about some surprising figures on male sexuality that he learned while working on his new comedy special, Big Divorce Energy.

You probably wouldn’t be surprised to hear that more than half of women surveyed admit to having faked an orgasm at some point, given how often those performances are referenced in TV shows and movies. But research consistently shows that men fake orgasms, too. One study found that around a quarter of men reported doing so.

Adam certainly found that stat surprising, and he’s spent a lot of time thinking about why—and going down rabbit holes about what other aspects of straight, male sexuality get taken for granted. If men aren’t willing to talk about the orgasms they fake, what else are they sweeping under the rug? Check out this week’s episode for more.

There’ve been dozens of reported cases of spontaneous human combustion throughout history, going as far back as 17th Century Europe and as recently as 2010, when 76-year-old Michael Faherty’s death in Galway, Ireland, sparked talk of this spooky phenomenon.

One famous 1731 account of Countess Cornelia Bandi’s untimely demise, written by a priest, Giuseppe Bianchini, is particularly harrowing. It describes just a few blackened bits and body parts remaining, amid the apparent and mysterious destruction of most of her body. Her lower legs allegedly remained intact (stockings and all!) while the rest was burned to greasy ash. It’s not surprising that Giuseppe’s tale took on a life of its own. After all, getting reduced to a pile of cinders and a pair of ankles is quite the way to go.

Famous authors, starting with Charles Dickens in Bleak House, took inspiration from these startling descriptions, which popped up in Enlightenment and Victorian-era tabloids. And Dickens, in particular, latched onto the idea—taking it as 100% fact that a human being could erupt in flames with no particular outside interference. In fact, Dickens was one half of a 10-month long, public debate about whether or not spontaneous human combustion is possible. Dickens and his friend, philosopher George Lewes, had a major disagreement over the science in the form of back and forth published letters and installments of Bleak House, where Dickens would routinely defend spontaneous human combustion in the introduction to each chapter.

Since Dickens helped to popularize and defend the phenomenon, it’s stayed persistent among a certain set of conspiracy theorists and pseudoscientists. There are lots of ideas about how and why a person might suddenly burst into flames out there, from lightning strikes, intestinal gases, acts of God, and even ketosis. But the truth is likely a little sadder, if not stranger.

The prevailing scientific wisdom suggests most of these mysterious deaths are the outcome of the “wick effect.” Under the right conditions, some people basically burn like candles. Thanks to experiments with pig carcasses, blankets, and one woman’s osteoporitic bones at the Tennessee Body Farm, we know that an elderly person wearing the wrong clothes at the wrong time near an open flame can unfortunately burn long enough and hot enough to destroy most of a body, bone and all, without necessarily igniting a house fire.

#4555. Genesis GV60 Magma Doesn’t Sacrifice Speed for Faux-Shift Fun

Unlike its Ioniq 5 N fraternal twin, the electric Genesis GV60 Magma is just as quick simulating shifts as in its standard drive mode.

Welcome to Car and Driver's Testing Hub, where we zoom in on the test numbers. We've been pushing vehicles to their limits since 1956 to provide objective data to bolster our subjective impressions (you can see how we test here).

When the Hyundai Ioniq 5 N arrived on the scene back in 2023, it introduced simulated shifting to electric vehicles. We were so enthralled by its combustion-engine cosplay that it played a major part in the 5 N being named our 2024 EV of the Year. As fun as it is to bang through gears in a vehicle without an engine, our testing proved that the 5 N’s acceleration times significantly suffered in “N e-Shift” mode compared with its standard drive mode. Like the Ioniq 5 N, the new Genesis GV60 Magma—the luxury brand’s first entry in its performance-focused Magma sub-brand—features a “Virtual Gear Shift” mode that mimics the sensations of an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic paired to an internal-combustion engine. But this time, it doesn’t come at a performance cost.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 63129

Beneath the surface, the Ioniq 5 N and the GV60 Magma feature nearly identical hardware. Both are built on Hyundai Motor Group's E-GMP electric vehicle platform, feature a dual-motor all-wheel drive powertrain that produces up to 641 horsepower, make use of an 84-kWh battery pack, and both roll on 275/35R-21 Pirelli P Zero Elect tires, although the Magma gets newer PZ5-spec rubber versus the Ioniq 5 N’s PZ4 Pirellis. Besides the GV60 Magma’s nearly four-inch-shorter wheelbase and 91-pound-heavier curb weight, the differences between the pair are primarily software-related or matters of styling and design.

Some of those discrepancies are superficial—the 5 N’s faux-engine soundtrack mimics a 7750-rpm inline-four while the Magma’s aural signature is based on a 9000-rpm V-6, for example—but others have an impact on performance. Both models can only access their max power output with a time-limited Boost mode, and while the Hyundai can maintain its 641-hp peak in 10-second bursts, the Genesis can continue at full tilt in 15-second increments. That longer duration of peak output allows the Magma to walk away from the 5 N as they approach their Vmax—for example, the Genesis beats the Hyundai to 150 mph by almost two seconds—but otherwise the two were bumper-to-bumper up to 120 mph. The real delta between the Hyundai and Genesis’s straight-line capabilities only surfaces once both are switched into their simulated-shift drive modes.

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 Magma for sale near 63129

The last time we had an Ioniq 5 N at our test track, we performed two separate acceleration runs, once without N e-Shift and once with it activated. Importantly, N e-Shift mode disables the 5 N’s N Grin Boost and launch-control features, essentially robbing it of 40 horsepower and an optimized start, so we conducted the first run without launch control to even the playing field a bit. Still, the 5 N proved to be significantly quicker when it wasn’t hammering through make-believe gears, silently rocketing to 60 mph in 3.1 seconds, reaching 100 mph in 7.2 seconds, and crossing the quarter-mile marker in 11.3 seconds. With N e-Shift activated, it took the Ioniq 5 N 3.5 seconds to reach 60 mph (a four-tenth increase), 8.3 seconds to hit 100 mph (a whopping 1.1 seconds slower than in its standard drive mode), and 11.8 seconds to clear the quarter-mile (five-tenths behind our non-N e-Shift run).

When we conducted the same experiment in the GV60 Magma, we got very different results. During our testing, the Magma achieved nearly identical acceleration figures regardless of its drive mode. In both of its runs, the Genesis managed a 3.0-second sprint to 60 mph, a 6.8-second dash to 100 mph, and a quarter-mile time of 11.0 seconds. (The 0.1-second difference between our reported quarter-mile time of 11.1 seconds for the Magma and the 11.0-second figure quoted here is that, in this case, we were comparing two runs in the same direction, while all of our official acceleration figures are an average of a run in each direction.)

Given that the 5 N and Magma feature nearly identical specs and that all other environmental factors were equal, what gives? To us, the answer seems pretty straightforward. Unlike in the 5 N, engaging the Magma’s Virtual Gear Shift mode doesn’t lock out its boost or launch-control functions, allowing it to access its full 641-hp output and a “6000-rpm,” traction-aided takeoff whether it is fake shifting or not. The additional 40 horsepower and better getaway also explain why the Genesis’s fake-shift acceleration figures are far better than the Hyundai’s, with the Magma beating the 5 N to 60 mph by 0.5 second, to 100 mph by 1.5 seconds, and to the quarter-mile by 0.8 second. Ultimately, the Ioniq 5 N forces you to choose between its primary party trick and peak performance, while the GV60 Magma lets you have your cake and eat it too.

#4554. The 2027 BMW 740 xDrive Builds on Excellence

Revised design and an updated interior sharpen the case for BMW’s biggest executive sedan.

BMW’s 7-series has been in a race with the Mercedes-Benz S-class for nearly 50 years over the German executive sedan crown. But an avant-garde, new-generation reimagining in 2022 knocked the long-wheelbase sedan off its pedestal. Four years later, BMW has tweaked the 7-series’s front and rear design and upgraded the interior with better technology. Also, it’s lost the “i” from the end of its badge, as part of BMW’s new policy on model naming. Can a shorter name, a prettier face, and new screens push it back into contention?

Our expert editors test every vehicle we review. Read more about how we test and review cars here.

The 2027 BMW 740 xDrive’s most significant change is apparent at first glance. Horizontal grille slats inside the sizable kidney grille replace the previous vertical ones. Split headlights stick around, with a new vertical, indented integration below the daytime running lights. Extended LED taillights are also new for 2027. Inside, the BMW 740 receives much of the same treatment that’s been given to the Neue Klasse EV models, including a new four-spoke steering wheel, a snappier operating system, and a sleek panoramic display.

Engine: turbocharged and mild-hybridized 2998-cc inline-six

Transmission: 8-speed automatic, all-wheel drive

In the hills above Lake Elsinore, the 740 xDrive showed off just how magically BMW’s adaptive chassis control system is, especially in its more able Professional guise. This uses full air suspension and active roll stabilization through an electrical system that applies torque against the sway bars to counter lean under cornering loads. So equipped, the 7-series rewarded a spirited pace on California canyon roads, despite a 4800-pound curb weight sitting atop a 126.6-inch wheelbase.

Front-end turn-in was sharp, and the minuscule amount of body roll effectively hid the magnitude of weight swinging around. Like many recent BMWs, the steering was nicely weighted but largely mute, forcing dynamic awareness to come from the base of the seat instead of through my fingers. While plentiful electronically ordered handling adjustments were no doubt happening in real time, these intrusions felt imperceptible behind the wheel.

But the 740 isn’t a one-trick pony, either. Out on the highway, the 7-series serves a different customer. The same roll stabilization technology that keeps it planted in the canyons can decouple the roll bars for straight-line driving, reducing unwanted movements in the cabin and allowing the air suspension to soften even more. The result was a ride that felt effortlessly smooth over freeway joints but never turned wallowing. Luxury vehicles shouldn’t translate bumps and dips inside the cabin, and the 740 expertly balances stability at the wheel with a supple experience in the rear seat. Cruising at California highway speeds was where the 7-series felt truly at home.

Similarly, the turbocharged and electrified 3.0-liter inline-six engine is powerful and smooth, but certainly not shouty. With 394 hp, the 740 has the same power as a base-model X5, but it didn’t feel lacking at the helm. The 398-lb-ft torque peak comes in at 1850 rpm, which pushed the big sedan along gracefully without apparent effort. But winding the engine to the 5200 rpm at which peak power arrives elicited a pleasant, if speaker-amplified, song—although it felt largely unnecessary given the muscle of the torque curve.

Paired with the ever-amicable ZF eight-speed automatic transmission, the powertrain of the 740 felt like a means to an end rather than a especial highlight, but that’s how most buyers of large luxury sedans will expect it to be. Sure, you can paddle-shift through the gears and enjoy the gearbox’s satisfyingly snappy responses, but how many owners are likely to regularly do so?

BMW is proud of its hands-free Highway Assistant semiautonomous driving system, and so I put this to the test on I-5 South. The SAE Level 2 system can drive hands-free up to 85 mph as long as you keep a forward gaze, and it did so well. From slowing for construction zones to autonomous lane changes, the semiautonomous system handled busy California traffic smartly and smoothly.

My only real complaint with the updated 7-series was its soft brake pedal. Even with the sizable standard rotors, the soft pedal tuning made the heavy sedan feel underbraked, requiring more force than I was expecting to need to apply for a quick stop. Plus, like most of the R&T team who have encountered it, I don’t like the new four-spoke steering wheel with its strange disconnected spokes and awkward haptic touch controls.

With a mild facelift and the same powertrains as before, the 2027 7-series’s most noticeable upgrades are all inside. BMW uses many buzzwords and acronyms to describe the new interior experience, but the most important one is the Panoramic iDrive system. As in the X5, iX3, i3, and new 3-series, the Neue Klasse direction has removed the old physical iDrive controller and replaced it with a fully touchscreen system. The 7-series now has a 17.9-inch central screen, a recessed 14.6-inch passenger display, and the long panoramic gauge cluster that sits atop the dashboard.

In practice, the new user experience was a mixed bag. I’m quick to criticize any vehicle that lacks tactile controls, and the glamour of BMW’s new system doesn’t belie this fault. Save for a scrolling volume control near the nub shifter, everything from climate control to vehicle settings must be manipulated through the central touchscreen. The screen responds quickly and has a permanent menu with obvious icons for climate control, vehicle settings, navigation, and media inputs. However, tapping on any of these icons once is only the start of a multistep process, much of which will be done with eyes off the road.

To adjust the suspension or ride height on the 740, I had to click through four menus before the change was complete. Even the seat’s lumbar support has to be adjusted through the touchscreen. That’s a bridge too far in my book.

Despite these annoyances, BMW’s new system mostly excels at providing driving information with the projected gauge cluster. Illuminated on a span of masked glass across the dashboard, this instrument display was perfectly placed and kept my field of vision clear. BMW’s projection direction is smartly tuned, with speed placed directly in front of the driver and navigation to the right. Interesting but superfluous information like elevation is projected nearer to the passenger side. My only real complaint was a hard-to-decipher tachometer.

My Frozen Purple 740 xDrive was well appointed with white Merino leather seats that were heated, cooled, and massaging. The seating experience was unimpeachably comfortable except for the loud fan noise while using the ventilation function. Seating adjustment is now done through door-mounted buttons, allowing BMW to make the seats even wider. The equipped Dolby Atmos system was predictably excellent, and interior sound levels were nearly silent even without active tunes.

As brands like Audi and Lexus move away from the ultraluxury sedan market, BMW’s 7-series is left with a single natural competitor—the Mercedes-Benz S-class. But the fight isn’t exactly equal, either. The 740 starts at $101,350 in a rear-wheel-drive configuration, while the most affordable S-class starts at $114,100. Mercedes offers more horsepower and torque for the money, but the luxury-sedan buyer is unlikely to be motivated exclusively by performance.

Of course, if they are, then the 740 sits at the base of the range, with both the hybrid 750e and twin-turbo V-8 M760 positioned above it. Plus, of course, the continued novelty of the fully electric i7 EV, which shares the same bodywork.

Far be it from me to pretend reviewing a BMW 7-series is hard work, but the massaging seat feature certainly helped me calm down after hours of driving. BMW offers a variety of intensity settings and location-focused massages, meaning you can tailor the experience to where you need it most. It isn’t too hard or unnatural-feeling, and it still provides genuine relief.

#4553. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4552. Relaxed bear wins award for luxurious eating style—underneath an Alaskan waterfall

Published Nov 4, 2026 11:13 AM EST

Typically, when a bear catches a nutritious salmon, they don’t eat it under a rushing waterfall. But one unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) eating at Anan Creek in Alaska’s Tongass National Forest decided to park underneath a waterfall and enjoy his fishy snack.

For this culinary innovation, the U.S. Forest Service team at Tongass National Forest has awarded the unnamed bear with the 2026 Shower Beer award.

“After watching this relaxed black bear gnawing on a salmon under rushing waters, we’re wondering if it might catch on—like the ursine equivalent of the shower beer,” the team writes. “The more you watch, the more sense it makes. No mess and no need to move to start fishing again. This bear may be on to something.”

The rangers at Tongass National Forest are currently awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendanhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Like their beefy counterparts further to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return annually each summer to eat salmon and teach their cubs how to fish and survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own habits and quirks.

The U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted here, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

#4551. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

#4550. Man builds robotic cat feeder that senses when dish is empty

Published Nov 4, 2026 12:00 PM EST

Pet owners can pick from any number of automatic cat feeders at this point, and even shell out hundreds of dollars for a particularly fancy kit. But at the end of the day, most of them are simply a scooper that dumps out premeasured amounts of feline food based on an internal timer.

Jason Winfield, a New Zealand-based YouTuber and frequent traveler, wanted a slightly more advanced option: a robotic cat feeder that distributes a predetermined amount of food for his two pals, and also senses when the dish is actually empty.

“I tried a few of those automatic feeders off-the-shelf, and look, they’re fine. They do the job. Sort of,” Winfield explains in his recent video. “But here’s what bothered me: How do I know my cat actually ate?”

Winfield’s invention is designed to avoid overfeeding or accidentally building a mountain of kibble. The device runs on a Raspberry Pi Pico with Wi-Fi capabilities, and includes a tiny LCD screen and a buzzer to alert when food has been delivered. An onboard real-time clock (RTC) module keeps time even without direct power, which allows for a timed feeding window for daily rations.

Winfield also attached a 3D-printed cat head toggle to cycle through settings on the feeder’s screen. DIY projects like this are bound to run into errors, so Winfield also encoded a failsafe that turns off the feed dispenser if the dish has remained full for a specific length of time.There’s even an ultrasonic sensor to detect the presence of a cat, so the feeder doesn’t inadvertently drop kibble on their head.

The end result is an efficient, reliable automatic feeder that keeps Winfield’s cats happy. Winfield himself is even confident that his cats will never go hungry while he’s traveling.

#4549. Mercedes-Benz Asks: What If We Put Screens in a Car’s Windows, Too?

New window display technology could unlock the opportunity to include even more screens in Mercedes automobiles.

If there’s a space to insert a screen, the folks at Mercedes-Benz will find it. And turns out, the carmaker’s engineers have found what they consider the next frontier to be conquered: your car’s windows. On Tuesday, Mercedes released previews of two new types of window displays, one called Intelligent Display in Glass and the other named Holographic Display.

The “Intelligent Display in Glass” essentially puts LED display elements directly into the vehicle windows. Why? Mercedes says warning symbols or traffic-related information could be displayed on the rear window to warn those behind you. One might presume brake lights do the trick of letting folks know you’re slowing down, but the examples Mercedes shows are much more specific as to the reason you’re slowing down; the glass can project the symbol of a car accident, pedestrian crossing, or all sorts of other things.

Our favorite is the text that simply reads “KEEP DISTANCE.” Could that potentially just enrage a tailgater even more? Sure, but it’s also objectively funny to have your car tell people behind you to back off.

Mercedes says it’s investigating two different LED technologies for this application. Mini LEDs are best-suited to larger displays in the rear window; meanwhile, Micro LEDs could be used on smaller areas to show animations, thanks to their higher resolution capabilities.

Examples of Micro LEDs in action are shown in the side window screens, where the car can display messages to its driver like battery charge status or a simple “goodbye” as you walk away. In both cases, when no content is displayed, Mercedes says the display elements laminated into the glass composite “remain almost invisible.” The “almost” there gives us some pause, so we’ll have to see it in person in order to make a judgement.

The other tech Mercedes previewed is the Holographic Display, which looks a bit like a HUD on steroids. A projector in the instrument panel would project content onto a new windshield that uses a special transparent film laminated into the glass. Mercedes says the display will be viewable only at specific viewing angles—the driver wouldn’t be able to see what’s projected in front of the passenger, and vice versa. The carmaker says this means the passenger could be watching a film projected onto the windshield, while the driver is shown navigation information.

In pictures, at least it’s better than a HUD in that the display looks like a projection you might see in a home theater setup. You get full color and a sharp image, though the examples that the carmaker showcases aren’t exactly too enticing, being images of Mercedes vehicles and the weather.

Just like the other displays shown in this preview, Mercedes says all of these ideas simply demonstrate potential future approaches. None of them are likely to end up in a production car any time soon, as they’re all currently under development. That said, now would be the time to sound off and let Mercedes know if any of the above is something you’d want in a car one day ... or not.

#4548. 2027 Genesis GV60 / GV60 Magma

See all results for new 2027 Genesis GV60 for sale near 20147

Genesis’s smallest SUV is the electric GV60, which is offered in a variety of flavors from the tame rear-wheel drive base model to the wild, 641-hp Magma performance trim. While the standard model is set up primarily for comfort, the GV60 Magma adds plenty of aggression to the formula.

Driving range for the base rear-wheel-drive model is highest in the bunch at 306 miles per charge. Going with all-wheel drive or the Magma trim reduces driving range dramatically, but all models offer quick charging times thanks to a robust 800-volt architecture.

Expert Tip: Genesis makes it clear that the ultimate goal of the GV60 Magma is to offer a sophisticated take on performance, melded with plenty of luxury rather than rip-your-guts-out performance; if EV ferocity is your sole desire, check out the Ioniq 5 N.

Compare the 2027 Genesis GV60 with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

The GV60 Magma is a new variant this year, spearheading the GV60’s push into the performance EV class. It replaces last year’s Performance trim. 2027 also sees the introduction of an all-wheel-drive Prestige trim that bridges the gap between the base GV60 model and the new Magma.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

The rear-wheel-drive GV60 Standard gets motivation from a single rear-mounted 225-hp motor; going with all-wheel drive adds a front motor for a combined 314 horsepower. The GV60 Magma boosts output to 641 ponies.

The GV60's road manners are quite refined. When cruising, the cabin remains whisper quiet; encounter a stretch of winding road, though, and the GV60 offers enough athleticism to entertain the driver and enough surefootedness to inspire confidence. The chassis has been recalibrated for the Magma with specific damper and power distribution metrics, along with chunky 275/35R-21 tires specially developed for the Magma by Pirelli.

In addition to Launch Control and Boost mode, drivers have a choice of three additional drive modes: Sprint, GT, and MY, the latter allowing for customization of the electronically controlled limited-slip differential, stability control, and other performance factors. There's also a drift mode, but Genesis is careful not to call it a "drive" mode for normal street use. When we drove the GV60 Magma, we found it to be nimble in the corners and more polished than the Ioniq 5 N.

In Comparison: The Ioniq 5 N, with an identical 641 horsepower in Boost mode, also ripped to 60 mph in 3.0 seconds in our testing.

Although most buyers likely won't hook a trailer up to the GV60, it can tow up to 2000 pounds.

The GV60 uses a lithium-ion battery with 84 kW of usable capacity. The rear-wheel-drive base model offers the most range at 306 miles per charge, while the Magma trim offers the least at 220 miles. In our real-world 75-mph highway range test, the Magma went just 200 miles. DC fast charging is available, with Genesis claiming the GV60 can be replenished from 10-to-80 percent in just 18 minutes. C/D testing corroborates this claim, as our test vehicle replenished the battery from 13 percent to 80 percent in 18 minutes. Genesis says a level 2 AC charger can replenish the battery from 10 to 100 percent in about seven hours.

The EPA estimates that the rear-wheel drive GV60 should deliver up to 119 MPGe city, 101 MPGe highway, and 110 MPGe combined. All-wheel-drive models are rated for up to 107 MPGe city, 93 MPGe highway, and 100 MPGe combined. The Magma is rated for 84 MPGe city, 72 MPGe highway, and 78 MPGe combined. MPGe stands for miles per gallon of gas equivalent, an EPA metric that estimates PHEV and EV fuel efficiency. For more information about the GV60's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: Though the Genesis GV60 isn't as spacious as its larger GV70 and GV80 siblings, it offers a slightly more modern interior that embraces the high-tech concept. Whereas the GV70 and GV80 take a more traditional luxury approach, the GV60 integrates some cool motifs and features, including a center-console gear selector that flips upside down when in park and has the appearance of a crystal ball. The Magma model gets a unique look all its own, with the seats, doors, and the center console sporting synthetic suede upholstery highlighted with Magma Orange and grey stitching. A Magma-exclusive steering wheel features orange accents on the control buttons.

Second Row: Rear seat space and comfort are expected to be the same as the non-Magma GV60, but we wouldn’t rule out more aggressive bolstering that might make fitting three across difficult or impossible.

Cargo Capacity: Behind the GV60 Magma's rear seat is a 24.0-cubic-foot cargo bay. With the rear seats folded, that cargo volume grows to 54.7 cubic feet. A tiny frunk offering just 0.71 cubes of storage resides under the SUV's hood. With all the seats up, the standard GV60 accommodated seven carry-on bags in C/D testing.

A large 27.0-inch touchscreen display stretches across the GV60 Magma's dashboard. It provides room for a digital gauge cluster as well as a central infotainment screen. Bluetooth, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, in-dash navigation, a head-up display, and a wireless smartphone charging pad are all standard. An eight-speaker stereo is standard; a premium Bang & Olufsen setup with 17 speakers is optional.

All GV60 Magma models come fully loaded with Genesis's driver-assistance features, including parking sensors, blind-spot monitoring, lane-keeping assist, and a lane-centering feature.

For information about the GV60’s crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Genesis warranty coverage exceeds the typical term limits for the luxury segment. The GV60 comes with powertrain coverage for up to 10 years or 100,000 miles and complimentary scheduled maintenance for three years or 36,000 miles.

#4547. EcoFlow’s new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations keep a reserve of extra power for emergencies

Published Nov 4, 2026 1:24 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’ve ever driven with white knuckles to a gas station while your car’s range read “0 miles,” you’ll appreciate a new feature on this portable power station. EcoFlow is building a similar cushion into its new DELTA Gen4 portable power stations. A feature called Emergency Power Mode holds back a small reserve for charging phones after the screen hits 0 percent.

Two models are on sale today through EcoFlow’s website: the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at an early-bird $1,299 and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, against list prices of $1,699 and $2,199. Both put out 3,600 watts in chassis EcoFlow says are smaller and lighter than its DELTA 3 Ultra models, which include the DELTA 3 Ultra Plus we tried last year. They arrive a month after EcoFlow’s TITAN home batteries targeted whole-home backup.

A power station spends some charge just keeping its inverter awake. EcoFlow rates both DELTA Gen4 models at 14 watts with the AC outlets switched on and nothing plugged in, and 3 watts in standby. At 14 watts, a full day of idling uses 336 watt-hours, about 11 percent of the DELTA 3000 Gen4’s 3,072Wh battery.

The 3-watt standby number is what lets EcoFlow claim a fully charged DELTA 3800 Gen4 can sit for about 52 days before it drains, which matters for one parked in a closet waiting for an outage. EcoFlow pairs the lower overhead with a mode called Fridge Runtime Boost and rates the DELTA 3000 Gen4 for up to 58 hours of refrigerator runtime. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 gets more than 70 hours.

Those fridge numbers come from EcoFlow’s own tests with an empty 654-liter Samsung refrigerator, and the company notes that food load, room temperature, and door openings all change the result. The mode also supports one compressor-based appliance, such as a fridge or freezer, at a time, and EcoFlow says not to run other AC loads alongside it. We haven’t tested either DELTA Gen4 model yet, so these performance figures are EcoFlow’s. Emergency Power Mode covers what’s left after the battery runs down. You turn it on from the unit or the EcoFlow app, and EcoFlow says the reserve can give an iPhone 17 nearly a full extra charge.

Both DELTA Gen4 models share a 16.8 x 11.4-inch footprint, and both are rated for 3,600 watts continuous and 7,200 watts of surge from their 120V outlets. That’s enough to run a 1,500-watt space heater and a refrigerator at the same time with room to spare. EcoFlow’s original DELTA Pro weighed about 99 pounds to hit the same 3,600-watt rating.

The DELTA 3800 Gen4 fits 691 extra watt-hours and about 10 more pounds into the same footprint, for 3,763Wh at 67.5 pounds. EcoFlow says that’s roughly 33 pounds lighter than the DELTA Pro, and it holds slightly more energy. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 holds 3,072Wh at 57.3 pounds, and EcoFlow puts it at about 20 percent lighter than the DELTA 3 Ultra, with the same capacity.

The bigger model also has more ways to grow. The DELTA 3800 Gen4 takes up to 2,000 watts of solar across two inputs and has an expansion port for up to two extra batteries, including the DELTA Pro 3 Smart Extra Battery, for about 12kWh total. The DELTA 3000 Gen4 has one 1,000-watt solar input, and its spec sheet lists no battery port.

EcoFlow says the DELTA 3000 Gen4 refills from a wall outlet in under two hours and the DELTA 3800 Gen4 in under 2.5 hours. The 3kWh, 3,600-watt class is crowded, with Anker’s SOLIX F3000 and Jackery’s Explorer 3000 v2 at the same capacity and output. Our guide to the best portable power stations covers the field.

The DELTA 3000 Gen4 and DELTA 3800 Gen4 are listed for preorder. As of November 4, EcoFlow shows the DELTA 3800 Gen4 shipping in late November and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 in early December.

EcoFlow’s early-bird pricing runs through December 7. That puts the DELTA 3800 Gen4 at $1,699, 23 percent off its $2,199 list, and the DELTA 3000 Gen4 at $1,299, which is $400 below its $1,699 list.

For a house that needs a fridge, a router, and a few lamps through a weekend outage, this is the DELTA to look at first. It has the same 3,600-watt output as its bigger sibling and weighs about 10 pounds less. The savings come out of expandability, since it gets one 1,000-watt solar input, four charging methods, and no listed battery expansion.

At early-bird prices, $400 more buys 691 extra watt-hours, a second 1,000-watt solar input, and an expansion port that takes the system to about 12kWh with add-on batteries. That port is the reason to step up if you plan to expand a home-backup system later. EcoFlow rates it for more than 70 hours on a refrigerator and lists six ways to charge it.

#4544. California has way more bugs than we thought

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:00 PM EST

It’s true that there are more insects on Earth than any other animal. They make up roughly 80 percent of the planet’s animals and include about 900,000 known species. However, those jaw-dropping numbers can make it easy to undercount our six-legged friends. Take the state of California. Over 60,000 different species of insects reside in the Golden State, and scientists have only described about two-thirds of them. A study published today in the journal Ecography details the findings, which represents a huge bump in the estimated number of insects in California.

The study is part of the California Insect Barcode Initiative (CIBI), a $6 million project to collect and identify every species of insect in the state. Multiple institutions including the California Department of Food and Agriculture, UC Berkeley, UC Riverside, San Diego Natural History Museum, the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco, and Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County (NHM) worked together to DNA barcode over one million insect specimens.

To build the insect library, the team gathered tissue samples from museum collections and caught living insects in 72 ecoregions around the state. Ecoregions are places that have similar ecosystems as defined by the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). They also undertook research expeditions to 454 additional locations across California, and used Malaise traps to gather the insects. Malaise traps passively capture bugs, but require a bit of work to maintain.

“This is an example of community science. Volunteers stepped forward to help with sampling by managing traps, which we would not have been able to do for continuous weekly sampling,” Giar-Ann Kung, a study co-author and NHM Entomology collections manager, said in a statement.

The study looked at Level 3 ecoregions, which include places like the Mojave Basin and Range, Southern California Mountains, and Sierra Nevada. They found that the Mojave Basin and Range have the highest insect species richness.

The team also compared parallel ecoregions and found that each one is home to its own unique mix of insect life, even if they have a similar climate and geography. While there are parallels between locations within the same ecoregion, the team found that the richness of life across California is more abundant and more delicate than previously thought. Researchers say that these results highlight the need for more aggressive conservation of California’s wild places to protect the insects living there.

#4543. Toyota’s Corolla Cross EV spotted for the first time [Images]

Toyota is giving its best-selling Corolla a major makeover, and an all-electric version is part of the plan. The upcoming Corolla Cross EV was captured in public for the first time ahead of its expected 2027 debut.

The Corolla has always been “a car for everyone,” Toyota’s former president and current CEO, Koji Sato, said after unveiling the next-gen Corolla Concept at last year’s Japan Mobility Show.

Since it went on sale 60 years ago, over 57 million drivers have chosen the Corolla, making it Toyota’s best-selling vehicle ever.

The Corolla has undergone 12 model changes since 1966, but the compact car is about to undergo its biggest transformation yet.

Although it’s still a top seller, the Corolla has lost some of its appeal as new, more advanced, and efficient options have emerged. Toyota looks to change that with the next-generation model.

It will remain “a car for everyone,” as Sato said, but the next-gen Corolla will come in multiple powertrains, including an all-electric version.

“Whether it’s a battery EV, plug-in hybrid, hybrid, or internal combustion engine vehicle―whatever the power source―let’s make good-looking cars that everyone will want to drive,” Sato said at the Japan Mobility Show last October.

Ahead of its expected debut sometime in 2027, a disguised Corolla Cross EV was spotted driving near Toyota’s European headquarters and R&D center.

New images from Chinese media outlet Autohome show what’s expected to be the all-electric Corolla Cross, with a closed-off grille and a unique body design.

The new Corolla will be the first to use Toyota’s new “multipathway” platform that will support electric, hybrid, gas, and other powertrains.

Toyota hasn’t revealed specifics, including battery or powertrain specs, but the next-gen Corolla EV is expected to remain close in style to the Concept. Aside from the massive COROLLA badge on the back, it looks like an entirely different vehicle with a near sports-car-like silhouette.

In an exclusive interview with Japanese media NHK in July, Toyota’s current chairman and former CEO, Akio Toyoda, warned that the company “cannot survive” if it does not adapt amid new competition and technology from China.

During the special, which went behind the scenes at Toyota’s “top secret” development site, several blurred Corolla Concept body types, including a sedan, hatchback, crossover, and GR model, were revealed in the background.

According to a recent Nikkei report, Toyota plans to begin production of the next-gen Corolla in 2028 through its joint venture with Chinese state-owned FAW Group, FAW Toyota Motor.

The Toyota Corolla EV is expected to be available in single- and dual-motor configurations with a driving range of at least 250 miles.

Let's hope that Toyota gets the Corolla EV right, because if it offers the right range for the right price but still feels fundamentally like a Corolla it is an EV that would get consideration from buyers who wouldn't otherwise consider an EV.

They're the buyers that trust Toyota and who consider the Corolla to be a nice safe choice for a car. And by safe, that means a vehicle that may not be all that exciting, but also a vehicle that they won't regret buying. Needless to say, these are not people who read Electrek, or even Car & Driver, for that matter. But there's a lot more of them than there are of us.

The hybrid version will reportedly use a new 1.5-liter four-cylinder engine and an electric motor. Toyota’s engineers told Car and Driver the system would deliver around 134 horsepower. It’s also estimated to be 10% to 20% more efficient than the current Corolla.

Toyota has yet to confirm the electric version will launch in the US. According to Car and Driver, the gas version will likely start at around $25,000, the hybrid around $27,000, and the EV and PHEVs will likely be priced in the $30,000 range.

A clean car is a happy car, but you need the right vacuum to keep things tidy. (As an outdoor adventurer and proud pet owner, I know this all too well.) So, do I really need a special vacuum just for my car? Yes. That’s why I was excited to put a fleet of top-rated car vacuums to the test on a dusty Porsche Boxster at our garage in New Jersey. After deciding which units we wanted to focus on, we assessed suction power, ease of use, hose length, portability, attachment versatility, and overall quality. A good vacuum should make detailing effortless, not frustrating.

Whether you just want to tidy up or are a serious detailer, these are the car vacuums that stood out in our hands-on testing. Each proved they can handle everything from fine road dirt to the stubborn fur of a rambunctious dog. If it made our list, it’s because we’d use it ourselves.

More Car-Care Gear: Best Leather Car Cleaners | Best Upholstery Cleaners | Best Interior Cleaners

The Metrovac Vac N Blo isn’t just a car vacuum. This machine is a steel-bodied detailer with a 4-hp motor that delivers serious suction and blower power. The two flexible six-foot hoses aren’t flimsy plastic cords; they’re made with a pro-grade material for those who take cleaning seriously.

Right out of the box, it impressed with its array of attachments: two extension wands, four deluxe micro-detailing attachments, a blower nozzle, a pick-all upholstery nozzle, a dust brush, and a crevice tool.

Whether you’re dealing with deep-seated pet hair, stubborn crumbs, or layers of dust, this vacuum does its job with ease. There was a noticeable difference even after just one go-over on the floor mat. The Vac N Blo never felt like it struggled, wherever we were vacuuming.

When you need to dry your car or blast grit out of vents, the blower function is just as powerful, making it a true two-in-one garage essential. I used this setting to blow the bits of dirt and gravel right out of the garage door.

It also allows you the option to attach wheels, making it even easier to maneuver. In this case, I attached the shoulder strap and had it move with me as I worked my way around the mats and car. It’s also a very sleek design—it looked sharp in the garage and stood out not just in performance but also in aesthetics.

Beyond its power, the all-metal construction gives it a level of durability you won’t find in typical car vacuums. The long hose and multiple attachments make tackling every inch of your interior easy, turning a once-dreaded task into a precision operation. If you want a vacuum that’ll deliver professional-level results, the Metrovac Vac N Blo is the one to get.

The DetailVac is the smallest on the list, and it was also the easiest to work with. It plugged right into the Boxster’s 12-volt outlet and, at only three pounds, was easy to maneuver. The 16-foot cord is long enough to accommodate a bigger vehicle with multiple seats or crevices. Overall, it does what it states but doesn’t excel.

While it picked up most of the dust and dirt on the floor mats, it left behind pet fur and debris. The vacuum includes three attachments that are helpful in harder-to-reach spots: The crevice tool worked well, but the brush tool didn’t do much for puppy fur. A flexible connection hose also acts as an extended hose, but it seemed to diminish the suction power when added. It’s not as powerful as the others we tested, which makes sense given its size.

I liked that an additional air filter was included. Depending on how often you use the vacuum, the filters can last up to six months without needing a change, but it’s nice that an extra one is provided.

Overall, the DetailVac is convenient and great for quick cleanups or accidents. I think it would be especially helpful if you have kids.

The Bissell Garage Pro Wall-Mounted Wet/Dry Vacuum is for anyone serious about keeping their car and garage clean. Mounted on your wall with a 32-foot hose, it delivers strong 12-amp suction to tackle dirt and wet spills. There’s a blower option, perfect for drying off a freshly washed Porsche, which I did with stellar results.

Even at its size, assembly was simple. Once it’s together, it performs at the level you’d expect from a professional detailing station. This is the best pick if you have the room and use a vacuum in your garage often. It’s a full-service garage vacuum built to take a beating and deliver strong suction for any surface of your vehicle.

What also sets it apart is its auto-tool kit, which includes attachments—crevice tools, upholstery brushes, and a wet nozzle for moisture cleanup—for every cleaning scenario.

Whether you’re an obsessive detailer or just want a cleaner ride, the Garage Pro delivers. It is powerful, versatile, and a worthwhile addition to any garage.

Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum packs a lot of power for a smaller unit. I quickly understood why most people use the wall-mount option; not only does it help keep the 30-foot hose out of the way, but it also helps keep your garage organized. If I had mounted this, the hose probably would’ve been less cumbersome to maneuver. Drilling holes in our space to mount several vacuums was not an option, but we did our best to re-create this real-world scenario. Assembly was a bit of a struggle—especially getting the central hose in—but I might not have used enough force initially. My advice would be to use all your strength; I promise you won’t break it.

The suction is decent, with 120 volts of power, but the attachments really help this vacuum shine: steel telescoping wand, bare-floor tool, snake wand, crevice tool, elongated dust brush, and upholstery tool. They make this vacuum even more versatile, allowing you to tackle everything from floor mats to delicate surfaces efficiently.

Using this vacuum was genuinely satisfying, like power-washing your interior with suction. Adam’s did indeed get the job done fast, and had it been wall-mounted, I think I would’ve seen its overall appeal, since using the hose would likely be more manageable. Adam’s Polishes Wall-Mounted Vacuum is worth every penny for those who love organization.

The Shark StainForce isn’t your typical car vacuum, and that’s precisely why we wanted to include it. Rather than tackling loose dirt, this cordless spot cleaner focuses on stubborn oil stains, soda spills, and odors embedded in your car’s carpeting.

There’s a three-step cleaning process involved, but it’s well worth the extra work. Spray the affected area with Shark’s dual-activated cleaning solution, scrub with the included attachment, and use the vacuum’s suction to extract the mess. The dual-chamber formula mixes when sprayed, helping break down stains without requiring any measuring or extra preparation. Two attachments, including a crevice tool, make it easier to reach tight spaces around seats and other interior surfaces.

Weighing under three pounds, the StainForce is easy to maneuver, and its cordless design eliminates the hassle of finding an outlet. The included storage caddy keeps everything organized between cleanups.

There are a few limitations. Battery life topped out at approximately 20 minutes when we tested (so it still works fine for spot cleaning). Also, you’ll need to purchase Shark’s own cleaning solution when the included supply runs out.

For drivers regularly battling coffee spills, muddy footprints, or pet accidents, the StainForce offers a convenient, targeted cleaning solution.

A high-quality vacuum cleaner can make all the difference for keeping your car’s interior spotless. Unlike household vacuums, car-specific models are designed to tackle heavier debris in tight spaces. However, with so many options available, choosing the right one can be overwhelming. It’s important to consider key features that affect performance and convenience to make an informed decision.

Three of the most crucial factors to evaluate are suction power, which determines how effectively the vacuum picks up dirt; attachments and accessories, which help clean hard-to-reach areas; and the power source, which impacts portability and run time.

Understanding these features will help you find a vacuum that best suits your needs, whether you prioritize strong suction for deep cleaning, versatile tools for detail work, or the malleability of a hose. Let’s dive into these essential features to ensure you choose the right car vacuum cleaner for the job.

Suction power is the most critical factor in a car vacuum because vehicle interiors can become a nightmare with everything we drag in and out of them. Unlike home carpets, car surfaces are filled with a million little spaces, textured upholstery, and stubborn floor mats that anything you can think of clings to. A vacuum with weak suction won’t be able to extract dirt that’s ground into these surfaces, leaving your car looking only half clean. Not ideal.

Additionally, higher suction power means faster, more efficient cleaning. Instead of repeatedly going over the same spot, a strong vacuum gets the job done in fewer passes, saving you time and effort. It also helps tackle heavier things such as leaves, sand, or pebbles. If you take your car’s cleanliness seriously (or don’t want to spend forever vacuuming), a high-powered vacuum is the way to go.

Attachments and accessories are essential in a car vacuum because car interiors are full of tight spaces and tricky surfaces that a standard nozzle can’t handle. Unlike home vacuums, which deal with flat carpets and open areas, a car vacuum must navigate between seats, air vents, and cup holders, all of which require specialized tools.

For example, a crevice tool helps reach between and along door panels, while a brush attachment is perfect for loosening dust from dashboards. Wide nozzles quickly work on large areas like a trunk, and wet/dry tools handle accidents before they become permanent stains. The right attachments don’t just make cleaning easier; they ensure you’re getting every last crumb out of your ride, leaving it truly spotless.

The power source of a car vacuum determines its suction strength, mobility, and convenience. Corded (AC-powered) vacuums offer the strongest suction but require an outlet and may limit movement. Cordless (battery-powered) models provide maximum portability for quick cleanups but often have weaker suction and limited run time.

Vacuums that plug into a car’s 12-volt outlet are great for on-the-go use but generally lack the power of AC models. Choosing the right type depends on your needs, such as going corded for power, cordless for convenience, or 12-volt for in-car accessibility.

The ThisWorx portable car vacuum routinely came up as the one to avoid. Its low suction didn’t do much, leaving most of the dirt and dust behind. While it is inexpensive, you do indeed get what you pay for.

The same goes for generic no-name vacuums on Amazon. While they are more affordable, they are also unreliable and often break within months of purchase.

We focused on suction power, attachments, and ease of use for this test. Using substantially dirty floor mats as our starting point, we taped them off to determine which vacuum was the most powerful. These mats were full of dirt, dust, pebbles, and dog fur; they were pretty much littered with what you might encounter in your vehicle. This strategy helped us quickly determine which vacuums were up to the task.

Our garage in New Brunswick, New Jersey, was the ideal backdrop for this test. Not only was it still dirty from summer trips, it also allowed me to spread out the old and very used floor mats I’d be using. While this test focused on how effectively the vacuums would clean up cars, a happy surprise was that they also cleaned the garage.

For this test, we reached out to pros to see what products they prefer. After determining fan favorites, digging around forums, and connecting with detailers we’ve worked with in the past, we devised a list of items to review. (You know you’re headed in the right direction when you hear the same brand or product come up multiple times.) This is how we arrived at Chemical Guys, Adam’s, Bissell, and Shark—solid and reliable brands. Metrovac popped up in my digging as a reliable shop vac in a popular Reddit group (r/AutoDetailing). They weren’t wrong.

We didn’t look at handheld car vacuums in this test. While they’re tops for convenience, they would be a separate category to investigate, given their variety. We did keep convenience in mind when picking the units we wanted to focus on, but this test was done with serious garage owners and car enthusiasts in mind.

When we reviewed the Car+Boat from Dyson, we were immensely impressed at how well the mini-vac lived up to its brand’s legacy. With legendary suction power, the Dyson was as much a revelation for car lovers as the company’s larger vacuums were for homeowners all those years ago.

Portable, lightweight, and affordable. What more could you want in a car vac? With a 20-volt MAX Li-ion battery and extra-long crevice tool, it’s as great for the car as it is around the house.

Looking for a little more power than a portable cordless vacuum can provide? Pick up this mini-utility shop vac from Armor All. It’s far more convenient than lugging around a larger shop vac, has a washable filter, and doubles as a blower.

When choosing a car or garage vacuum, size and capacity are crucial factors that impact performance and convenience. A vacuum with anywhere from two to six gallons of capacity is usually sufficient for car detailing, providing enough volume for typical debris while remaining lightweight and portable. Smaller vacuums are easier to maneuver inside a car and can be stored conveniently in a garage or trunk.

A 10-plus-gallon shop vacuum is better for garage use or frequent heavy-duty cleaning. These larger models can handle bigger messes, including sawdust, metal shavings, and wet spots, without requiring frequent emptying. They also typically feature more powerful motors for increased suction. However, they take up more storage space and may be less portable. If you need a balance between power and maneuverability, a mid-size vacuum can provide strong suction without being too bulky.

While a regular household vacuum might seem convenient for cleaning your car or garage, it often lacks the necessary power, durability, and specialized attachments for effective cleaning in these environments. Household vacuums are designed primarily for indoor surfaces such as carpets and hardwood floors, meaning they may struggle to pick up messes commonly found in cars and garages. Their shorter hoses and bulkier designs can make it challenging to reach tight spaces.

Dedicated car vacuums and shop vacuums are better suited for these tasks, offering more powerful suction, longer hoses, and attachments specifically designed for automotive cleaning. These vacuums are built with durability, often featuring rugged designs that can withstand dust, moisture, and rough handling in a garage setting. While household vacuums may work in a pinch for light cleaning, investing in a purpose-built car or garage vacuum ensures more efficient cleaning and a longer-lasting machine.

HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters are essential when purchasing a car or garage vacuum, especially if you are concerned about air quality. Standard vacuum filters may struggle to trap fine particles such as dust, pollen, pet dander, and mold spores, which can get released back into the air during cleaning.

HEPA filters, however, are designed to capture at least 99.97 percent of particles, making them highly effective at reducing allergens and airborne contaminants. This is particularly beneficial if you suffer from allergies.

For car and garage cleaning, a HEPA or high-efficiency filtration system can also help keep your vehicle’s interior and your garage workspace cleaner by preventing fine dust from resettling. While HEPA-filtered vacuums may be slightly more expensive, they offer significant benefits for maintaining a healthier environment.

#4540. Why a pink potato-like robot is wheeling around Philadelphia

Published Nov 4, 2026 2:17 PM EST

It was a showdown worthy of a classic Western, except the things rolling down the street weren’t tumbleweeds. They were robots.

On one side of an Old City sidewalk in Philadelphia, an Uber Eats robot trundled along on its daily route. Suddenly, something blocked its path, and it was met face-to-interface with another, new robot. This new bot on the block was wildly different from its utilitarian, food-conveying counterpart: Not only did it have blond hair, blue eyes, and a perpetually lolling tongue, but it also had a name. Meet Orifice the Awebot.

Meg Saligman, founder of the Ministry of Awe, an immersive art installation located in a 19th-century Old City bank building, had raced ahead to intercept the bot so Orifice could meet it. According to The Philadelphia Inquirer, Orifice’s creator, Madison Polidoro, then joked that the two robots were “gonna fight!”

The Uber Eats robot chose a pacifist approach, steering around its would-be adversary without incident.

But Orifice wasn’t created to instigate a territorial dispute between robots. She was made to promote peace between robots and humans, which is no small feat in the City of Brotherly Love. Here, delivery bots aren’t brothers. They’re the “other,” even when they’re bringing you a cheesesteak with Whiz.

Since Uber Eats delivery bots made their Philadelphia debut in March, the city has not exactly rolled out the red carpet. Within weeks of the robots’ launch, Philadelphians displayed “the whole spectrum” of reactions, according to Dr. Philip Dames, an associate professor of mechanical engineering at Temple University in Philly.  Most people barely gave them a second glance, but on the extreme end, one robot was kicked over at around midnight, and one was sat on and graffitied with the words, “DESTROY ME PLZ.”

Orifice was designed to be a more warmhearted, interactive answer to the joyless functionality of delivery bots. But why are some people compelled to harass delivery bots in the first place? And can a pink potato with a tongue change that?

The Ministry commissioned Polidoro, a Philadelphia-area fine artist and fabricator known as 10 Ton Fetus for her surreal and psychological sculptures, to create a mobile sculpture.

After talking it over with her colleagues, she decided to build her own robot, Orifice, as a foil to the Uber Eats bots.

“Having run into them, and being horrified by it, I was excited at the prospect of making their archnemesis, a hero of sorts!” she says. “Something perfectly opposite of what they [delivery robots] are.”

Polidoro knew that to properly offset the slick, appliance-like look of the Uber Eats bots, she would need to give Orifice plenty of human flourishes.

“She had to be cute, friendly, and human,” Polidoro says. “I carefully considered approachability and anchoring points for human connection in her design.”

Orifice stands two feet tall and is shaped like a potato. She has pink, weatherproof rubber skin, and large blue eyes that blink regularly and can also be remotely operated. Her dangling tongue, tuft of Troll doll-esque blond hair, and pink ribbon juxtaposed with an occasional top hat give her a quirky, sometimes unsettling charm.

And yes, her name is literal: She has what Polidoro calls a “functional orifice” on her rear end, a common feature of the artist’s work.

For a city that has officially embraced the grotesque hockey mascot Gritty, which The Guardian has described as “an acid trip of a mascot,” Orifice almost seems like a love letter on wheels. And so far, the reaction to Orifice has been largely positive, Polidoro says.

“Most people smile, laugh and record her, asking questions and wanting to know more,” she says. “Occasionally, people are surprised or find her a bit unsettling. But even those people seem curious and lighthearted.”

Unlike the delivery bots, which Polidoro describes as “something from a science fiction novel,” Orifice seems to hit a sweet spot in terms of adorableness.

“She seems to tap into the psychology of cuteness, like a dog or a child, something understood to be precious and innocent,” she says. (Fortunately, Orifice seems to stop short of provoking “cute aggression,” the urge to squeeze something unbearably adorable.)

And there truly is a psychology of cuteness. Researchers have found that robots designed with the “baby schema” (big eyes, round faces, and other infant-like features) are perceived as cuter and more trustworthy. Research by Kate Darling, a robot ethicist who studied human/robot interaction at the MIT Media Lab for about 15 years, has also found that names and backstories make people hesitate to hurt robots, Dames notes. But a pretty face can only go so far.

“A face alone doesn’t protect a robot,” Dames says. “The Uber Eats rovers have blinking, winking eyes and still got hazed, and a face engineered to look friendly can read as manipulative.”

And that’s not the only way making a robot more “humanlike” can backfire, according to Dr. Donald Hantula, a professor of psychology and neuroscience at Temple University. He likens it to Star Wars’ beloved beep-bot R2-D2 versus the frequently beleaguered, all-too-humanoid C-3PO. The more a robot resembles us, he suggests, the more likely it is to face the bullying we usually reserve for one another.

“The problem is that the more human something becomes, the more we tend to treat it as human-like,” he says. “And we humans have a really terrible history of how we treat fellow members of our species.”

So, will Orifice manage to strike the perfect balance between human and machine, serving as an ambassador of goodwill between tech-weary humans and the machines rolling into their neighborhoods?

So, what is driving hostility toward robots on the street? Whatever it is, Philadelphia seems to have a lot of it. In 2015, hitchBOT, a robot built for a social experiment on the kindness of strangers, was found decapitated at the top of Old City’s Elfreth’s Alley. Named after local blacksmith and property owner Jeremiah Elfreth, the alley is considered one of the oldest continuously inhabited residential streets in the United States.

The alley’s museum has since hosted events about hitchBOT’s demise that are part commemoration, part celebration, with an annual festival possibly in the works.

But hostility toward robots is far from just a Philly thing, or even a delivery bot thing, Dames notes.

“I’d expect friction wherever robots enter public space without local say,” he told Popular Science.

That invasion of space without public buy-in can be especially challenging on crowded public sidewalks, which robots must share, as Dames puts it, “with kids, dogs, wheelchair users, and tourists, none of whom opted in.” On those packed sidewalks, the robots are, in Hantula’s words, “essentially beer coolers on wheels” and consistently “get in people’s way.”

Can apps really make you fluent in another language?

Do water picks really work? Dentists weigh in.

Beyond these logistical issues, Dames says, robots on the street are often among the only physical manifestations of the otherwise inaccessible corporate entities they represent.

“The robot is the only part of a company a person can physically reach,” he says. “You can’t confront a cloud algorithm or a board of directors, but you can confront the rover on your block.”

Facing down delivery bots is precisely what Dr. Carolyn Marvin, a retired University of Pennsylvania communications professor, has been doing. On Oct. 14, Marvin was arrested and cited for disorderly conduct after stationing herself in front of an Uber Eats robot near Reading Terminal Market. It wasn’t the first time she’d blocked the bots on her daily walks.

Marvin told KYW Newsradio that she’s protesting “the ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers.” She says she has no intention of stopping.

Confronting robots may also offer an outlet for modern anxieties about the rapid, seemingly ungovernable ascent of artificial intelligence, which some experts have warned could wipe out humanity within a decade. Some passersby have even been known to yell “clanker,” an insult popularized by Star Wars that has since become an anti-AI slur, at Uber Eats bots.

“The physical embodiment gives you a better target in a sense,” Hantula says. “It’s really hard to kick against AI, but it’s like, okay, I see that thing and I can.”

And some of it might be simply for show, Hantula notes.

“A lot of this I think is also driven by getting social media likes,” he says.

Yet some cultures do seem able to coexist peacefully with delivery bots and other robots. In Korea and Japan, for example, robots are viewed as reliable, time-saving helpers, not professional rivals or harbingers of doom.

Orifice probably won’t be able to single-handedly repair the troubled history of robot/human relations in America, but perhaps her presence will provide, as her name suggests, an opening.

“Sometimes it can be, and needs to be, as simple as a moment of raw discovery and joy, savoring the little things that make us human,” Polidoro says. “I’d like Orifice to bring a piece of that [joy and discovery] to everyone she encounters.”

#4539. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

Heatpumps over here have been able to do this for years already.

And it's not one of two signals. Inverter controlled HP's enables control of the effect, and not just "normal or boost".

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs.
